AA3D85A0DFE301310DD468A86D17958E.description: Analyze a case in which two or more texts provide conflicting information on the same topic and identify where the texts disagree on matters of fact or interpretation.

AA3D3160DFE301310DD368A86D17958E.description: Delineate and evaluate the argument and specific claims in a text, assessing whether the reasoning is sound and the evidence is relevant and sufficient; recognize when irrelevant evidence is introduced.

AA3CC3E0DFE301310DD268A86D17958E.description: Evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of using different mediums (e.g., print or digital text, video, multimedia) to present a particular topic or idea.

AA3C0C50DFE301310DD068A86D17958E.description: Determine an author's point of view or purpose in a text and analyze how the author acknowledges and responds to conflicting evidence or viewpoints.

AA3BAFD0DFE301310DCF68A86D17958E.description: Analyze in detail the structure of a specific paragraph in a text, including the role of particular sentences in developing and refining a key concept.

AA3B5D20DFE301310DCE68A86D17958E.description: Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in a text, including figurative, connotative, and technical meanings; analyze the impact of specific word choices on meaning and tone, including analogies or allusions to other texts.

AA3AAF10DFE301310DCC68A86D17958E.description: Analyze how a text makes connections among and distinctions between individuals, ideas, or events (e.g., through comparisons, analogies, or categories).

AA3A5CB0DFE301310DCB68A86D17958E.description: Determine a central idea of a text and analyze its development over the course of the text, including its relationship to supporting ideas; provide an objective summary of the text.

AA3A0310DFE301310DCA68A86D17958E.description: Cite the textual evidence that most strongly supports an analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text.

AA38DC00DFE301310DC768A86D17958E.description: By the end of the year, read and comprehend literature, including stories, dramas, and poems, at the high end of grades 6—8 text complexity band independently and proficiently.

AA388990DFE301310DC668A86D17958E.description: Range of Reading and Level of Text Complexity

AA3835C0DFE301310DC568A86D17958E.description: Analyze how a modern work of fiction draws on themes, patterns of events, or character types from myths, traditional stories, or religious works such as the Bible, including describing how the material is rendered new.

AA37D810DFE301310DC468A86D17958E.description: Analyze the extent to which a filmed or live production of a story or drama stays faithful to or departs from the text or script, evaluating the choices made by the director or actors.

AA36A050DFE301310DC168A86D17958E.description: Analyze how differences in the points of view of the characters and the audience or reader (e.g., created through the use of dramatic irony) create such effects as suspense or humor.

AA365140DFE301310DC068A86D17958E.description: Compare and contrast the structure of two or more texts and analyze how the differing structure of each text contributes to its meaning and style.

AA35FA40DFE301310DBF68A86D17958E.description: Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in a text, including figurative and connotative meanings; analyze the impact of specific word choices on meaning and tone, including analogies or allusions to other texts.

AA354F80DFE301310DBD68A86D17958E.description: Analyze how particular lines of dialogue or incidents in a story or drama propel the action, reveal aspects of a character, or provoke a decision.

AA34FA30DFE301310DBC68A86D17958E.description: Determine a theme or central idea of a text and analyze its development over the course of the text, including its relationship to the characters, setting, and plot; provide an objective summary of the text.

AA3492D0DFE301310DBB68A86D17958E.description: Cite the textual evidence that most strongly supports an analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text.

AA3384E0DFE301310DB868A86D17958E.description: Read and comprehend complex literary and informational texts independently and proficiently.

AA333960DFE301310DB768A86D17958E.description: Range of Reading and Level of Text Complexity

AA32EDC0DFE301310DB668A86D17958E.description: Analyze how two or more texts address similar themes or topics in order to build knowledge or to compare the approaches the authors take.

AA32A100DFE301310DB568A86D17958E.description: Delineate and evaluate the argument and specific claims in a text, including the validity of the reasoning as well as the relevance and sufficiency of the evidence.

AA324AF0DFE301310DB468A86D17958E.description: Integrate and evaluate content presented in diverse media and formats, including visually and quantitatively, as well as in words.
comments: Please see "Research to Build and Present Knowledge" in Writing and "Comprehension and Collaboration" in Speaking and Listening for additional standards relevant to gathering, assessing, and applying information from print and digital sources.

AA3199D0DFE301310DB268A86D17958E.description: Assess how point of view or purpose shapes the content and style of a text.

AA314980DFE301310DB168A86D17958E.description: Analyze the structure of texts, including how specific sentences, paragraphs, and larger portions of the text (e.g., a section, chapter, scene, or stanza) relate to each other and the whole.

AA30F3B0DFE301310DB068A86D17958E.description: Interpret words and phrases as they are used in a text, including determining technical, connotative, and figurative meanings, and analyze how specific word choices shape meaning or tone.

AA300570DFE301310DAE68A86D17958E.description: Analyze how and why individuals, events, and ideas develop and interact over the course of a text.

AA2FAE20DFE301310DAD68A86D17958E.description: Determine central ideas or themes of a text and analyze their development; summarize the key supporting details and ideas.

AA2F57D0DFE301310DAC68A86D17958E.description: Read closely to determine what the text says explicitly and to make logical inferences from it; cite specific textual evidence when writing or speaking to support conclusions drawn from the text.

AA2E9D60DFE301310DAA68A86D17958E.description: College and Career Readiness Anchor Standards for Reading

document.title: Alabama Course of Study: Arts Education Visual Arts

A3C09110DFE30131035B68A86D17958E.description: Compare the creative processes of visual arts with other arts disciplines, the humanities, and other academic areas.
comments: Examples: comparing creative problem-solving models with the scientific method, comparing the drafting process in writing with the composition process in visual arts

A3C1B040DFE30131035F68A86D17958E.description: Describing the social, cultural, historical, and political context of selected works of art
comments: Examples: impact of Jacque-Louis David's Oath of the Horatii on French society and painting styles, adoption of Greek temples as architectural models in later cultures

A3C1F460DFE30131036068A86D17958E.description: Describing the stylistic impact of selected works of art
comments: Examples: Claude Monet's Impression, Sunrise; Egyptian obelisk

A3C16B70DFE30131035E68A86D17958E.description: Explain the importance of major works of art and architecture.

A3C12490DFE30131035D68A86D17958E.description: Analyze artists' choices in order to interpret meanings, ideas, attitudes, views, and intentions in works of art.
comments: Examples: choice of media, subject matter, signs, symbols, source of inspiration

Examples: Francisco Goya's The Third of May and the Napoleonic Invasion of Spain, Diego Rivera's murals and the history of Mexico, Bayoux Tapestry and the Battle of Hastings, Native American paintings and the Battle of the Little Bighorn
A3C0DD40DFE30131035C68A86D17958E.description: Analyze specific works of art to determine the relationship between intrinsic qualities and historical and cultural context.

A3BFF2D0DFE30131035968A86D17958E.description: Interpret expressive intentions and purposes in selected works of art based on intrinsic and extrinsic conditions.
comments: Example: looking at Vincent Van Gogh's The Night Café and reading his letter to Theo about his intentions in creating the painting

A3BFA050DFE30131035868A86D17958E.description: Relate ideas of selected critics, historians, aestheticians, and artists to specific works of art.
comments: Examples: Harold Rosenburg on Willem de Kooning's action paintings; critical writings on contemporary art and artists in local, regional, and national periodicals; Public Broadcasting System's American Masters series on nineteenth-century American authors

A3BEEB80DFE30131035668A86D17958E.description: Organize an exhibition of works of art, including publicizing an exhibition, composing an exhibition statement, and completing a self-evaluation of an exhibition.
comments: Examples: exhibiting works of art on bulletin boards with content documentation, displaying works of art for competition, showcasing works of art with interdisciplinary connections in media centers
Example: using slides or electronic images to depict works of art

A3BDE140DFE30131035368A86D17958E.description: Writing an artist's statement for a personal portfolio

A3BE7C50DFE30131035568A86D17958E.description: Demonstrating advanced skill with at least three visual arts media

A3BD9C10DFE30131035268A86D17958E.description: Assemble a portfolio of personal works of art that includes a concentration in a specific theme or medium.

A3BD5620DFE30131035168A86D17958E.description: Defending personal choices in creative visual compositions
comments: Examples: oral critiques, written reflections

A3BD0B80DFE30131035068A86D17958E.description: Solving visual arts problems using analysis, synthesis, and evaluation

A3BCB340DFE30131034F68A86D17958E.description: Generating alternative design solutions to visual arts problems

A3BC6900DFE30131034E68A86D17958E.description: Organize subject matter and formal qualities into meaningful and expressive compositions.

A3BC2340DFE30131034D68A86D17958E.description: Describing the results of researching the works of other artists or cultures for inspiration

A3BBDC00DFE30131034C68A86D17958E.description: Produce a thematically related body of work.

A3BAE690DFE30131034968A86D17958E.description: Organize research about art, artists, cultures, times, and places into a product or presentation.
comments: Examples: producing a digital presentation comparing the use of logos in advertising, writing a research paper comparing art and its social context

A3BA9070DFE30131034868A86D17958E.description: Compare modes of artistic expression used in art and other academic disciplines.
comments: Examples: comparing improvisation in music, visual arts, dance, and theatre; comparing narrative art to literature, a painting of historic events to social sciences, op art to the science of optics, or tessellations to geometric shapes and designs

A3B9E770DFE30131034668A86D17958E.description: Comparing works of art with different styles
comments: Examples: Celtic knot designs with rose windows, African masks with Kabuki masks

A3BA3C40DFE30131034768A86D17958E.description: Describing characteristics of works of art that are common to a cultural group or historical period
comments:
Examples: cultural—use of animals in Eskimo masks, absence of representations of animals or human form in Islamic art;
historical—inclusion of concepts of war and politics in Francisco de Goya's paintings

A3B99900DFE30131034568A86D17958E.description: Explain purpose, function, and meaning of selected works of art from a variety of cultures, times, and places.

A3B8C230DFE30131034368A86D17958E.description: Respond orally and in writing to ideas of selected critics, historians, aestheticians, and artists.
comments: Example: discussing criteria for valuing works of art from Kenneth Clark's What is a Masterpiece?

A3B86530DFE30131034268A86D17958E.description: Producing a reflective narrative that critically analyzes the organizational effectiveness and artistic choices of personal and peer works of art

A3B81F10DFE30131034168A86D17958E.description: Describing visual and functional qualities of composition

A3B7D860DFE30131034068A86D17958E.description: Analyzing selected works of art for visual and functional differences
comments: Example: comparing decorative ceramic vessels and utilitarian pottery

A3B79220DFE30131033F68A86D17958E.description: Apply the four-step process of critical analysis to works of art, including describing what is seen, analyzing how each artist arranged the elements of art and principles of design, interpreting expressive intent and purpose, and judging the effectiveness of communication.

A3B6FA50DFE30131033D68A86D17958E.description: Maintaining a self-directed sketchbook or journal

comments: Example: researching masks of various cultures to determine emotional and stylistic characteristics that might influence or inspire the making of a mask
A3B6B0F0DFE30131033C68A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate independent research related to studio work.

A3B66800DFE30131033B68A86D17958E.description: Produce a self-critique of a work in progress.

A3B61C90DFE30131033A68A86D17958E.description: Employ a diverse range of traditional media, digital media, multimedia, techniques, styles, tools, concepts, and processes in producing meaningful and expressive compositions.

A3B50930DFE30131033768A86D17958E.description: Producing a thematically related body of work

A3B5C7D0DFE30131033968A86D17958E.description: Employing a diverse range of traditional media, digital media, and multimedia; techniques; styles; tools; concepts; and processes in producing meaningful and expressive compositions

A3B57200DFE30131033868A86D17958E.description: Organizing subject matter and formal qualities in a work of art into meaningful and expressive compositions

A3B4BD70DFE30131033668A86D17958E.description: Selecting appropriate subject matter as a basis for meaningful and expressive compositions

A3B478D0DFE30131033568A86D17958E.description: Create works of art that communicate specific concepts, emotions, and intentions.

A3B1AC20DFE30131032C68A86D17958E.description: Compare ways of producing, responding, and understanding in the visual arts with other arts disciplines, the humanities, and other academic subject areas.
comments: Examples: process of writing compared to process of forming works of art; rhythms in visual arts, dance, and music compared to rhythms in poetry; color theory in art compared to color theory in science

A3B37B50DFE30131033268A86D17958E.description: Identifying arts careers in business and industry
comments: Examples: dance—choreographer, dance educator; music—conductor, composer; theatre—set designer, artistic director; visual arts—textile designer, museum curator

A3B31A50DFE30131033168A86D17958E.description: Identify various uses of the visual arts in business and industry.
comments: Examples: developing logos and advertisements, designing buildings and other structures

A3B2CE50DFE30131033068A86D17958E.description: Using a variety of resource media in researching stylistic characteristics of selected art, artists, cultures, times, and places
comments: Example: creating a multimedia presentation, storyboard, poster, or research paper to identify characteristics of Jacob Lawrence's Harlem series paintings

A3B28760DFE30131032F68A86D17958E.description: Analyzing major works of art and architecture from various cultures, times, and places to understand forms, subjects, themes, and symbols
comments: Examples: Parthenon in Athens, Greece; Kremlin in Moscow, Russia

A3B24200DFE30131032E68A86D17958E.description: Describe stylistic characteristics of selected works of art and architecture.
comments: Examples: Raphael's (Raffaello Sanzio) Madonnas in the High Renaissance, Cathedral of Notre Dame in Gothic architecture, Charles Demuth's painting I Saw the Figure Five in Gold

A3B1FB10DFE30131032D68A86D17958E.description: Use appropriate visual arts terminology in response to works of art, including the elements of art and principles of design.

A3B0FF20DFE30131032A68A86D17958E.description: Interpreting the subject matter, purpose, and expressive content of a work of art

A3B0AA90DFE30131032968A86D17958E.description: Identifying the elements of art and principles of design

A3B05020DFE30131032868A86D17958E.description: Produce a reflective narrative that critically analyzes selected works of art.

A3AFFBA0DFE30131032768A86D17958E.description: Explaining the role of works of art placed in the environment
comments: Examples: Maya Lin's Vietnam Veterans Memorial in Washington, D.C.; Lin's Civil Rights Memorial in Montgomery, Alabama; AIDS (acquired immunodeficiency syndrome) Quilt Memorial; Robert Smithson's Spiral Jetty

A3AF96D0DFE30131032668A86D17958E.description: Describe various artistic contributions to environmental and social issues.
comments: Examples: Frederic Olmstead's design of Central Park, Frank Lloyd Wright's Falling Water, Jacob Lawrence's Migration series

A3AF05E0DFE30131032468A86D17958E.description: Comparing a finished personal work of art with its intended content or design

A3AF4F80DFE30131032568A86D17958E.description: Identifying criteria for judging works of art
comments: Examples: craftsmanship, originality, technique, content

A3AEBCA0DFE30131032368A86D17958E.description: Evaluate student works of art orally or in writing according to specified criteria.

A3AE2020DFE30131032168A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate safe handling of tools according to studio and environmental practices, procedures, and regulations.
comments: Examples: properly using and disposing of hazardous chemicals or fluids, using flame-retardant cabinets, utilizing ventilation systems

A3ADC210DFE30131032068A86D17958E.description: Demonstrating technical proficiency in the production and presentation of a work of art
comments: Examples: skillful use of printmaking tools, properly matting two-dimensional works of art

A3AD5240DFE30131031F68A86D17958E.description: Determining the appropriateness of techniques used to create a work of art

A3ACF900DFE30131031E68A86D17958E.description: Produce works of art using a variety of techniques.

A3AC5470DFE30131031C68A86D17958E.description: Describing how visual relationships create meaning in works of art

A3AC08E0DFE30131031B68A86D17958E.description: Organizing subject relationships in works of art
comments: Examples: mother and child, man-made objects in a landscape

A3ACAD10DFE30131031D68A86D17958E.description: Organizing formal relationships in works of art
comments: Examples: color contrasts, differences in shape and size, repetition of textures and patterns

A3ABC160DFE30131031A68A86D17958E.description: Create works of art with a variety of visual relationships.

A3AA1650DFE30131031568A86D17958E.description: Using digital processes or media to identify symbols and styles associated with works of art from various periods
comments: Example: using the Internet to view, collect, or find examples of Renaissance art and architecture

A3AABC10DFE30131031768A86D17958E.description: Describing the extrinsic context qualities of a work of art
comments: Example: optical color mixing theory as depicted in works by Berthe Morisot such as Jeune Fille au chien (Young Girl with a Dog)

A3AA6320DFE30131031668A86D17958E.description: Identifying the style associated with selected works of major artists
comments: Examples: Richard Estes—photorealism, Helen Frankenthaler—color field, Vincent van Gogh—post-Impressionism

A3A9C9F0DFE30131031468A86D17958E.description: Describe historical themes, symbols, and styles associated with works of art from various cultures, times, and places, including major periods and movements.

A3A973E0DFE30131031368A86D17958E.description: Describing the intrinsic qualities of a work of art
comments: Example: divisionist color in Camille Pissaro's Impressionist paintings

A3A90160DFE30131031268A86D17958E.description: Defining visual arts terminology to include the elements of art and principles of design

A3A8AA20DFE30131031168A86D17958E.description: Utilize specialized terminology from art history, aesthetics, criticism, and production in discussions of works of art.

A3A811F0DFE30131030F68A86D17958E.description: Identifying aesthetic components and formal qualities in man-made and natural objects
comments: Examples: comparing a Henry Moore sculpture with bones, comparing David Hockney's Grand Canyon series to rock formations

A3A79FF0DFE30131030E68A86D17958E.description: Compare works of art with functional and natural objects, aesthetic components, and formal qualities.
comments: Examples: stylized lines in automobiles; shapes and forms of appliances; shape, line, form, volume, and color of a tree

A3A74080DFE30131030D68A86D17958E.description: Describing the effectiveness of expressive and meaningful communication in selected works of art

A3A6B260DFE30131030B68A86D17958E.description: Interpreting expressive intentions and purposes in selected works of art

A3A6F950DFE30131030C68A86D17958E.description: Analyzing the formal organization of subject matter, elements of art, and principles of design in selected works of art to determine structural relationships

A3A66C60DFE30131030A68A86D17958E.description: Describing the subject matter, elements of art, principles of design, media, technique, and style used in selected works of art

A3A626C0DFE30131030968A86D17958E.description: Evaluate selected works of art to determine the effectiveness of their organization.

A3A5DEF0DFE30131030868A86D17958E.description: Describe personal, sensory, emotional, and intellectual responses to the visual qualities of a work of art.

A3A4FCF0DFE30131030568A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate safe and responsible handling of art materials, including cleanup, storage, and replenishment of supplies where applicable.

A3A4B630DFE30131030468A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate the use of traditional, digital, and multimedia techniques to create works of art.
comments: Examples: two-dimensional expression in books, comic strips, and timelines; enhancement of images in a digital imaging program; three-dimensional expression in dioramas, masks, puppets, mobiles, stabiles, scenery, and props

A3A46D60DFE30131030368A86D17958E.description: Apply the elements of art and principles of design to the production of two- and three-dimensional artwork.

A3A424E0DFE30131030268A86D17958E.description: Apply steps artists use in the production of art, including conceptualizing ideas and forms, refining ideas and forms, and reflecting on and evaluating both the process of production and the product.

A3A3C8A0DFE30131030168A86D17958E.description: Create original works of art using reflective ideas, personal experiences, and imaginary content.
comments: Examples: reactions to current events, cultural traditions, fantasy

A3A317C0DFE3013102FF68A86D17958E.description: Incorporating traditional categories of subject matter into original works of art
comments: Examples: drawing a still life, painting a landscape, sculpting a portrait

A3A2CB10DFE3013102FE68A86D17958E.description: Creating the illusion of three-dimensional forms through tonal rendering

A3A36B60DFE30131030068A86D17958E.description: Organizing spatial relationships utilizing linear and atmospheric perspective

A3A27C70DFE3013102FD68A86D17958E.description: Create original works of art from direct observation.

A3A155D0DFE3013102FA68A86D17958E.description: Identifying various art periods and movements
comments: Examples: periods—comparing Mayan temples and Egyptian pyramids or Renaissance and twentieth-century paintings, movements—comparing Impressionism and Cubism or Surrealism and Realism

A3A10A10DFE3013102F968A86D17958E.description: Describe historical and cultural influences on works of art.
comments: Examples: historical—creating a computer presentation depicting works of art of the Civil War, cultural—comparing the impact of racism in Faith Ringgold's Flag Quilt and William Johnson's Moon Over Harlem

A3A0BF50DFE3013102F868A86D17958E.description: Discuss ways in which the subject matter of other disciplines is connected with the visual arts.
comments: Examples: connection of plants and animals in a rainforest to Henri Rousseau's The Peaceable Kingdom; relationship of music to Wassily Kandinsky's paintings; relationship of measurement, scales, and proportion to Chuck Close's portraits

A3A07340DFE3013102F768A86D17958E.description: Define the appropriate technical terminology in creating a work of art.
comments: Example: explaining the terms greenware and bisque-fired when discussing the creation of a piece of pottery

A39FDBD0DFE3013102F568A86D17958E.description: Defining the four-step process of critical analysis, including describing what is seen, analyzing how each artist arranged the elements of art and principles of design, interpreting expressive intent and purpose, and judging the effectiveness of communication
comments: Example: analyzing Miriam Schapiro's The Poet #2 by asking "What do I see in the painting?," "How did the artist organize the elements of art and principles of design?," "What is the message that the artist is trying to convey?," and "How effective is the artwork?"

A39F94D0DFE3013102F468A86D17958E.description: Discuss strengths and weaknesses of a personal portfolio or other work of art.

A39F4D30DFE3013102F368A86D17958E.description: Apply appropriate vocabulary in discussing a work of art.
comments: Examples: discussing the use of cool colors, organic shapes, and flat perspective in Marc Chagall's Green Violinist; explaining movement in Giacomo Balla's Dynamism of a Dog on a Leash

A39EB680DFE3013102F168A86D17958E.description: Produce works of art using one- and two-point perspectives.
comments: Example: drawing a cityscape or still life of geometric shapes that uses a vanishing point and horizontal line

A39E1680DFE3013102EF68A86D17958E.description: Creating original works of art using observational skills
comments: Examples: drawing a shoe; painting a still life; creating a landscape in mixed-media; creating timed, gesture studies of a figure

A39DCE20DFE3013102EE68A86D17958E.description: Creating original multimedia works of art
comments: Examples: television broadcasts, digital imaging, multimedia presentations

A39E6490DFE3013102F068A86D17958E.description: Applying the elements of art and principles of design to the production of two- and three-dimensional artwork
comments:
Examples: two-dimensional—monochromatic paintings, found or natural object prints, texture-rubbing compositions;
three-dimensional—papier-mâchè masks, clay whistles

A39D8700DFE3013102ED68A86D17958E.description: Applying steps artists use in the production of art, including conceptualizing ideas and forms, refining ideas and forms, and reflecting on and evaluating both the process of production and the product

A39D3BA0DFE3013102EC68A86D17958E.description: Create works of art utilizing a variety of traditional and nontraditional media and techniques.
comments: Examples: torn-paper collage, weaving, wire sculpture, clay relief

document.title: Alabama Course of Study: Mathematics

AC6BBFA0DFE30131120768A86D17958E.description: Partition circles and rectangles into two and four equal shares, describe the shares using the words halves, fourths, and quarters, and use the phrases half of, fourth of, and quarter of. Describe the whole as two of, or four of the shares. Understand for these examples that decomposing into more equal shares creates smaller shares.

AC6B7A10DFE30131120668A86D17958E.description: Compose two-dimensional shapes (rectangles, squares, trapezoids, triangles, half-circles, and quarter-circles) or three-dimensional shapes (cubes, right rectangular prisms, right circular cones, and right circular cylinders) to create a composite shape, and compose new shapes from the composite shape.
comments: Students do not need to learn formal names such as "right rectangular prism."

AC6B2C10DFE30131120568A86D17958E.description: Distinguish between defining attributes (e.g., triangles are closed and three-sided) versus non-defining attributes (e.g., color, orientation, overall size); build and draw shapes to possess defining attributes.

AC6AD470DFE30131120468A86D17958E.description: Reason with shapes and their attributes.

AC6A3D20DFE30131120268A86D17958E.description: Organize, represent, and interpret data with up to three categories; ask and answer questions about the total number of data points, how many in each category, and how many more or less are in one category than in another.

AC69BD10DFE30131120068A86D17958E.description: Tell and write time in hours and half-hours using analog and digital clocks.

comments: Limit to contexts where the object being measured is spanned by a whole number of length units with no gaps or overlaps.
AC692B70DFE3013111FE68A86D17958E.description: Express the length of an object as a whole number of length units, by laying multiple copies of a shorter object (the length unit) end to end; understand that the length measurement of an object is the number of same-size length units that span it with no gaps or overlaps.

AC68D3C0DFE3013111FD68A86D17958E.description: Order three objects by length; compare the lengths of two objects indirectly by using a third object.

AC6895C0DFE3013111FC68A86D17958E.description: Measure lengths indirectly and by iterating length units.

AC681680DFE3013111FA68A86D17958E.description: Subtract multiples of 10 in the range 10-90 from multiples of 10 in the range 10-90 (positive or zero differences), using concrete models or drawings and strategies based on place value, properties of operations, and/or the relationship between addition and subtraction; relate the strategy to a written method and explain the reasoning used.

AC67D490DFE3013111F968A86D17958E.description: Given a two-digit number, mentally find 10 more or 10 less than the number, without having to count; explain the reasoning used.

AC678BA0DFE3013111F868A86D17958E.description: Add within 100, including adding a two-digit number and a one-digit number, and adding a two-digit number and a multiple of 10, using concrete models or drawings and strategies based on place value, properties of operations, and/or the relationship between addition and subtraction; relate the strategy to a written method and explain the reasoning used. Understand that in adding two-digit numbers, one adds tens and tens, ones and ones; and sometimes it is necessary to compose a ten.

AC673B50DFE3013111F768A86D17958E.description: Use place value understanding and properties of operations to add and subtract.

AC66F0E0DFE3013111F668A86D17958E.description: Compare two two-digit numbers based on meanings of the tens and ones digits, recording the results of comparisons with the symbols >, =, and <.

AC66AF10DFE3013111F568A86D17958E.description: The numbers 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80, 90 refer to one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, or nine tens (and 0 ones).

AC666BF0DFE3013111F468A86D17958E.description: The numbers from 11 to 19 are composed of a ten and one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, or nine ones.

AC661EC0DFE3013111F368A86D17958E.description: 10 can be thought of as a bundle of ten ones — called a "ten."

AC65CF00DFE3013111F268A86D17958E.description: Understand that the two digits of a two-digit number represent amounts of tens and ones. Understand the following as special cases:

AC651DE0DFE3013111F068A86D17958E.description: Count to 120, starting at any number less than 120. In this range, read and write numerals and represent a number of objects with a written numeral.

AC649760DFE3013111EE68A86D17958E.description: Number and Operations in Base Ten
comments: Grade 4 expectations in this domain are limited to whole numbers less than or equal to 1,000,000.

AC6454D0DFE3013111ED68A86D17958E.description: Determine the unknown whole number in an addition or subtraction equation relating three whole numbers.
comments: For example, determine the unknown number that makes the equation true in each of the equations 8 + ? = 11, 5 = - 3, 6 + 6 = .

AC640F70DFE3013111EC68A86D17958E.description: Understand the meaning of the equal sign, and determine if equations involving addition and subtraction are true or false.
comments: For example, which of the following equations are true and which are false? 6 = 6, 7 = 8 - 1, 5 + 2 = 2 + 5, 4 + 1 = 5 + 2.

AC63B4A0DFE3013111EB68A86D17958E.description: Work with addition and subtraction equations.

AC635A60DFE3013111EA68A86D17958E.description: Add and subtract within 20, demonstrating fluency for addition and subtraction within 10. Use strategies such as counting on; making ten (e.g., 8 + 6 = 8 + 2 + 4 = 10 + 4 = 14); decomposing a number leading to a ten (e.g., 13 - 4 = 13 - 3 - 1 = 10 - 1 = 9); using the relationship between addition and subtraction (e.g., knowing that 8 + 4 = 12, one knows 12 - 8 = 4); and creating equivalent but easier or known sums (e.g., adding 6 + 7 by creating the known equivalent 6 + 6 + 1 = 12 + 1 = 13).

AC631540DFE3013111E968A86D17958E.description: Relate counting to addition and subtraction (e.g., by counting on 2 to add 2).

AC629560DFE3013111E768A86D17958E.description: Understand subtraction as an unknown-addend problem.
comments: For example, subtract 10 - 8 by finding the number that makes 10 when added to 8.
Students need not use formal terms for these properties.
To add 2 + 6 + 4, the second two numbers can be added to make a ten, so 2 + 6 + 4 = 2 + 10 = 12. (Associative property of addition.)
If 8 + 3 = 11 is known, then 3 + 8 = 11 is also known. (Commutative property of addition.)
AC625270DFE3013111E668A86D17958E.description: Apply properties of operations as strategies to add and subtract.

AC621080DFE3013111E568A86D17958E.description: Understand and apply properties of operations and the relationship between addition and subtraction.

AC61C2E0DFE3013111E468A86D17958E.description: Solve word problems that call for addition of three whole numbers whose sum is less than or equal to 20, e.g., by using objects, drawings, and equations with a symbol for the unknown number to represent the problem.

AC6183B0DFE3013111E368A86D17958E.description: Use addition and subtraction within 20 to solve word problems involving situations of adding to, taking from, putting together, taking apart, and comparing, with unknowns in all positions, e.g., by using objects, drawings, and equations with a symbol for the unknown number to represent the problem.

AC614450DFE3013111E268A86D17958E.description: Represent and solve problems involving addition and subtraction.

AC60B7E0DFE3013111E068A86D17958E.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.
comments: Mathematically proficient students notice if calculations are repeated, and look both for general methods and for shortcuts. Upper elementary students might notice when dividing 25 by 11 that they are repeating the same calculations over and over again, and conclude they have a repeating decimal. By paying attention to the calculation of slope as they repeatedly check whether points are on the line through (1, 2) with slope 3, middle school students might abstract the equation (y – 2)/(x – 1) = 3. Noticing the regularity in the way terms cancel when expanding (x – 1)(x + 1), (x – 1)(x² + x + 1), and (x – 1)(x³ + x² + x + 1) might lead them to the general formula for the sum of a geometric series. As they work to solve a problem, mathematically proficient students maintain oversight of the process, while attending to the details. They continually evaluate the reasonableness of their intermediate results.

AC606A20DFE3013111DF68A86D17958E.description: Look for and make use of structure.
comments: Mathematically proficient students look closely to discern a pattern or structure. Young students, for example, might notice that three and seven more is the same amount as seven and three more, or they may sort a collection of shapes according to how many sides the shapes have. Later, students will see 7 × 8 equals the well remembered 7 × 5 + 7 × 3, in preparation for learning about the distributive property. In the expression x² + 9x + 14, older students can see the 14 as 2 × 7 and the 9 as 2 + 7. They recognize the significance of an existing line in a geometric figure and can use the strategy of drawing an auxiliary line for solving problems. They also can step back for an overview and shift perspective. They can see complicated things, such as some algebraic expressions, as single objects or as being composed of several objects. For example, they can see 5 – 3(x – y)² as 5 minus a positive number times a square and use that to realize that its value cannot be more than 5 for any real numbers x and y.

Mathematically proficient students try to communicate precisely to others. They try to use clear definitions in discussion with others and in their own reasoning. They state the meaning of the symbols they choose, including using the equal sign consistently and appropriately. They are careful about specifying units of measure, and labeling axes to clarify the correspondence with quantities in a problem. They calculate accurately and efficiently, express numerical answers with a degree of precision appropriate for the problem context. In the elementary grades, students give carefully formulated explanations to each other. By the time they reach high school they have learned to examine claims and make explicit use of definitions.

Mathematically proficient students consider the available tools when solving a mathematical problem. These tools might include pencil and paper, concrete models, a ruler, a protractor, a calculator, a spreadsheet, a computer algebra system, a statistical package, or dynamic geometry software. Proficient students are sufficiently familiar with tools appropriate for their grade or course to make sound decisions about when each of these tools might be helpful, recognizing both the insight to be gained and their limitations. For example, mathematically proficient high school students analyze graphs of functions and solutions generated using a graphing calculator. They detect possible errors by strategically using estimation and other mathematical knowledge. When making mathematical models, they know that technology can enable them to visualize the results of varying assumptions, explore consequences, and compare predictions with data. Mathematically proficient students at various grade levels are able to identify relevant external mathematical resources, such as digital content located on a website, and use them to pose or solve problems. They are able to use technological tools to explore and deepen their understanding of concepts.

Mathematically proficient students can apply the mathematics they know to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace. In early grades, this might be as simple as writing an addition equation to describe a situation. In middle grades, a student might apply proportional reasoning to plan a school event or analyze a problem in the community. By high school, a student might use geometry to solve a design problem or use a function to describe how one quantity of interest depends on another. Mathematically proficient students who can apply what they know are comfortable making assumptions and approximations to simplify a complicated situation, realizing that these may need revision later. They are able to identify important quantities in a practical situation and map their relationships using such tools as diagrams, two-way tables, graphs, flowcharts and formulas. They can analyze those relationships mathematically to draw conclusions. They routinely interpret their mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model if it has not served its purpose.

AC5F2F00DFE3013111DB68A86D17958E.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.
comments: Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases, and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and—if there is a flaw in an argument—explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.

Mathematically proficient students make sense of quantities and their relationships in problem situations. They bring two complementary abilities to bear on problems involving quantitative relationships: the ability to decontextualize—to abstract a given situation and represent it symbolically and manipulate the representing symbols as if they have a life of their own, without necessarily attending to their referents—and the ability to contextualize, to pause as needed during the manipulation process in order to probe into the referents for the symbols involved. Quantitative reasoning entails habits of creating a coherent representation of the problem at hand; considering the units involved; attending to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute them; and knowing and flexibly using different properties of operations and objects.

AC5E8300DFE3013111D968A86D17958E.description: Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them.
comments: Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. Older students might, depending on the context of the problem, transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on their graphing calculator to get the information they need. Mathematically proficient students can explain correspondences between equations, verbal descriptions, tables, and graphs or draw diagrams of important features and relationships, graph data, and search for regularity or trends. Younger students might rely on using concrete objects or pictures to help conceptualize and solve a problem. Mathematically proficient students check their answers to problems using a different method, and they continually ask themselves, "Does this make sense?" They can understand the approaches of others to solving complex problems and identify correspondences between different approaches.

document.title: Alabama Course of Study: Science

A5088050DFE30131053068A86D17958E.description: Describing various forms of technology used in observing Earth and its moon

A50831A0DFE30131052F68A86D17958E.description: Describe the position of Earth, the moon, and the sun during the course of a day or month.

A507DBF0DFE30131052E68A86D17958E.description: Recognizing the impact of society on human health and environmental conditions

A5077B00DFE30131052D68A86D17958E.description: Describe ways to sustain natural resources, including recycling, reusing, conserving, and protecting the environment.

A506F540DFE30131052B68A86D17958E.description: Organizing weather data into tables or charts

A5073360DFE30131052C68A86D17958E.description: Explaining symbols shown on a weather map

A506B5A0DFE30131052A68A86D17958E.description: Identifying technology used to record and predict weather, including thermometers, barometers, rain gauges, anemometers, and satellites

comments: Examples: positive—flooding deposits good soil when waters recede, negative—flooding kills crops
A5066EF0DFE30131052968A86D17958E.description: Identifying positive and negative effects of weather phenomena

A5061730DFE30131052868A86D17958E.description: Identifying cloud types associated with specific weather patterns

A505BAD0DFE30131052768A86D17958E.description: Identify conditions that result in specific weather phenomena, including thunderstorms, tornadoes, and hurricanes.

A5056F90DFE30131052668A86D17958E.description: Classifying rocks and minerals by characteristics, including streak, color, hardness, magnetism, luster, and texture

A5053200DFE30131052568A86D17958E.description: Describe Earth's layers, including inner and outer cores, mantle, and crust.

A5019BA0DFE30131051868A86D17958E.description: Determine habitat conditions that support plant growth and survival.
comments: Examples: deserts support cacti, wetlands support ferns and mosses

A504B420DFE30131052368A86D17958E.description: Describe how fossils provide evidence of prehistoric plant life.
comments: Example: plant fossils in coal or shale providing evidence of existence of prehistoric ferns

A5047480DFE30131052268A86D17958E.description: Identify how organisms are classified in the Animalia and Plantae kingdoms.

A50273F0DFE30131051B68A86D17958E.description: Identifying photosynthesis as the method used by plants to produce food

A502B440DFE30131051C68A86D17958E.description: Identifying helpful and harmful effects of plants
comments: Examples: helpful—provide food, control erosion; harmful—cause allergic reactions, produce poisons

A5034770DFE30131051E68A86D17958E.description: Classifying plants according to their features
comments: Examples: evergreen or deciduous, flowering or nonflowering

A5043230DFE30131052168A86D17958E.description: Describing how plants occupy space and use light, nutrients, water, and air

A503EB60DFE30131052068A86D17958E.description: Describing the role of plants in a food chain

A5022D50DFE30131051A68A86D17958E.description: Describe the life cycle of plants, including seed, seed germination, growth, and reproduction.

A501E0E0DFE30131051968A86D17958E.description: Identify structures and functions of the muscular and skeletal systems of the human body.

A5011810DFE30131051668A86D17958E.description: Identify the relationship of simple machines to compound machines.
comments: Example: pencil sharpener composed of a wheel and axle, inclined plane, and wedge
Examples: rubbing hands together, applying sandpaper to wood

A500D170DFE30131051568A86D17958E.description: Identifying forces that change an object's position or motion
comments: Examples: lifting, pushing, pulling

A4FF9AD0DFE30131051168A86D17958E.description: Identifying fossil fuels as a source of energy

A4FF5D40DFE30131051068A86D17958E.description: Describe ways energy from the sun is used.
comments: Examples: plant growth, light, heat
Examples: physical—chopping wood, chemical—burning wood
A4FF1E70DFE30131050F68A86D17958E.description: Identify physical and chemical changes of matter.

A4FEDF20DFE30131050E68A86D17958E.description: Classify substances as soluble or insoluble.
comments: Examples: soluble—sugar in water, powdered drink in water; insoluble—sand in water, oil in water

document.title: Alabama Course of Study: Mathematics

AD78C4D0DFE30131134468A86D17958E.description: Relating the choice of measures of center and variability to the shape of the data distribution and the context in which the data were gathered.

AD786E30DFE30131134368A86D17958E.description: Giving quantitative measures of center (median and/or mean) and variability (interquartile range and/or mean absolute deviation), as well as describing any overall pattern and any striking deviations from the overall pattern with reference to the context in which the data were gathered.

AD7821B0DFE30131134268A86D17958E.description: Describing the nature of the attribute under investigation, including how it was measured and its units of measurement.

AD778410DFE30131134068A86D17958E.description: Summarize numerical data sets in relation to their context, such as by:

AD771450DFE30131133F68A86D17958E.description: Display numerical data in plots on a number line, including dot plots, histograms, and box plots.

AD768200DFE30131133D68A86D17958E.description: Recognize that a measure of center for a numerical data set summarizes all of its values with a single number, while a measure of variation describes how its values vary with a single number.

AD763030DFE30131133C68A86D17958E.description: Understand that a set of data collected to answer a statistical question has a distribution which can be described by its center, spread, and overall shape.

AD75E8C0DFE30131133B68A86D17958E.description: Recognize a statistical question as one that anticipates variability in the data related to the question and accounts for it in the answers.
comments: Example: "How old am I?" is not a statistical question, but "How old are the students in my school?" is a statistical question because one anticipates variability in students' ages.

AD750FB0DFE30131133868A86D17958E.description: Use variables to represent two quantities in a real-world problem that change in relationship to one another; write an equation to express one quantity, thought of as the dependent variable, in terms of the other quantity, thought of as the independent variable. Analyze the relationship between the dependent and independent variables using graphs and tables, and relate these to the equation.
comments: Example: In a problem involving motion at constant speed, list and graph ordered pairs of distances and times, and write the equation d = 65t to represent the relationship between distance and time.

AD74C610DFE30131133768A86D17958E.description: Represent and analyze quantitative relationships between dependent and independent variables.

AD747670DFE30131133668A86D17958E.description: Write an inequality of the form x > c or x < c to represent a constraint or condition in a real-world or mathematical problem. Recognize that inequalities of the form x > c or x < c have infinitely many solutions; represent solutions of such inequalities on number line diagrams.

AD7421D0DFE30131133568A86D17958E.description: Solve real-world and mathematical problems by writing and solving equations of the form x + p = q and px = q for cases in which p, q and x are all nonnegative rational numbers.

AD73D230DFE30131133468A86D17958E.description: Use variables to represent numbers and write expressions when solving a real-world or mathematical problem; understand that a variable can represent an unknown number, or, depending on the purpose at hand, any number in a specified set.

AD738090DFE30131133368A86D17958E.description: Understand solving an equation or inequality as a process of answering a question: which values from a specified set, if any, make the equation or inequality true? Use substitution to determine whether a given number in a specified set makes an equation or inequality true.

AD7338A0DFE30131133268A86D17958E.description: Reason about and solve one-variable equations and inequalities.

AD72EF30DFE30131133168A86D17958E.description: Identify when two expressions are equivalent (i.e., when the two expressions name the same number regardless of which value is substituted into them).
comments: Example: The expressions y + y + y and 3y are equivalent because they name the same number regardless of which number y stands for.

Example: Apply the distributive property to the expression 3 (2 + x) to produce the equivalent expression 6 + 3x; apply the distributive property to the expression 24x + 18y to produce the equivalent expression 6 (4x + 3y); apply properties of operations to y + y + y to produce the equivalent expression 3y.
AD72A1A0DFE30131133068A86D17958E.description: Apply the properties of operations to generate equivalent expressions.

AD725AE0DFE30131132F68A86D17958E.description: Evaluate expressions at specific values of their variables. Include expressions that arise from formulas used in real-world problems. Perform arithmetic operations, including those involving whole-number exponents, in the conventional order when there are no parentheses to specify a particular order (Order of Operations).
comments: Example: Use the formulas V = s³ and A = 6 s² to find the volume and surface area of a cube with sides of length s = 1/2.
Example: Describe the expression 2 (8 + 7) as a product of two factors; view (8 + 7) as both a single entity and a sum of two terms.
AD720980DFE30131132E68A86D17958E.description: Identify parts of an expression using mathematical terms (sum, term, product, factor, quotient, coefficient); view one or more parts of an expression as a single entity.

AD71B5D0DFE30131132D68A86D17958E.description: Write expressions that record operations with numbers and with letters standing for numbers.
comments: Example: Express the calculation "Subtract y from 5" as 5 - y.

AD714D60DFE30131132C68A86D17958E.description: Write, read, and evaluate expressions in which letters stand for numbers.

AD70FDF0DFE30131132B68A86D17958E.description: Write and evaluate numerical expressions involving whole-number exponents.

AD70B850DFE30131132A68A86D17958E.description: Apply and extend previous understandings of arithmetic to algebraic expressions.

AD6EB440DFE30131132368A86D17958E.description: Solve real-world and mathematical problems by graphing points in all four quadrants of the coordinate plane. Include use of coordinates and absolute value to find distances between points with the same first coordinate or the same second coordinate.

AD6E7140DFE30131132268A86D17958E.description: Distinguish comparisons of absolute value from statements about order.
comments: For example, recognize that an account balance less than -30 dollars represents a debt greater than 30 dollars.

AD6E2A10DFE30131132168A86D17958E.description: Understand the absolute value of a rational number as its distance from 0 on the number line; interpret absolute value as magnitude for a positive or negative quantity in a real-world situation.
comments: For example, for an account balance of -30 dollars, write |-30| = 30 to describe the size of the debt in dollars.
For example, write -3 °C > -7 °C to express the fact that -3 °C is warmer than -7 °C.
AD6DDD70DFE30131132068A86D17958E.description: Write, interpret, and explain statements of order for rational numbers in real-world contexts.

comments: For example, interpret -3 > -7 as a statement that -3 is located to the right of -7 on a number line oriented from left to right.
AD6D8770DFE30131131F68A86D17958E.description: Interpret statements of inequality as statements about the relative position of two numbers on a number line diagram.

AD6D4140DFE30131131E68A86D17958E.description: Understand ordering and absolute value of rational numbers.

AD702C50DFE30131132868A86D17958E.description: Find and position integers and other rational numbers on a horizontal or vertical number line diagram; find and position pairs of integers and other rational numbers on a coordinate plane.

AD6FE040DFE30131132768A86D17958E.description: Understand signs of numbers in ordered pairs as indicating locations in quadrants of the coordinate plane; recognize that when two ordered pairs differ only by signs, the locations of the points are related by reflections across one or both axes.

AD6F8DD0DFE30131132668A86D17958E.description: Recognize opposite signs of numbers as indicating locations on opposite sides of 0 on the number line; recognize that the opposite of the opposite of a number is the number itself, e.g., -(-3) = 3, and that 0 is its own opposite.

AD6F3D40DFE30131132568A86D17958E.description: Understand a rational number as a point on the number line. Extend number line diagrams and coordinate axes familiar from previous grades to represent points on the line and in the plane with negative number coordinates.

AD6EF6C0DFE30131132468A86D17958E.description: Understand that positive and negative numbers are used together to describe quantities having opposite directions or values (e.g., temperature above/below zero, elevation above/below sea level, credits/debits, positive/negative electric charge); use positive and negative numbers to represent quantities in real-world contexts, explaining the meaning of 0 in each situation.

AD6CFB40DFE30131131D68A86D17958E.description: Apply and extend previous understandings of numbers to the system of rational numbers.

AD6CB250DFE30131131C68A86D17958E.description: Find the greatest common factor of two whole numbers less than or equal to 100 and the least common multiple of two whole numbers less than or equal to 12. Use the distributive property to express a sum of two whole numbers 1—100 with a common factor as a multiple of a sum of two whole numbers with no common factor.
comments: Example: Express 36 + 8 as 4 (9 + 2).

AD6C5DD0DFE30131131B68A86D17958E.description: Fluently add, subtract, multiply, and divide multi-digit decimals using the standard algorithm for each operation.

AD6C0760DFE30131131A68A86D17958E.description: Fluently divide multi-digit numbers using the standard algorithm.

AD6BA170DFE30131131968A86D17958E.description: Compute fluently with multi-digit numbers and find common factors and multiples.

AD6B5540DFE30131131868A86D17958E.description: Interpret and compute quotients of fractions, and solve word problems involving division of fractions by fractions, e.g., by using visual fraction models and equations to represent the problem.
comments: Examples: Create a story context for (2/3) ÷ (3/4) and use a visual fraction model to show the quotient; use the relationship between multiplication and division to explain that (2/3) ÷ (3/4) = 8/9 because 3/4 of 8/9 is 2/3. (In general, (a/b) ÷ (c/d) = ad/bc.) How much chocolate will each person get if 3 people share 1/2 lb of chocolate equally? How many 3/4-cup servings are in 2/3 of a cup of yogurt? How wide is a rectangular strip of land with length 3/4 mi and area 1/2 square mi?

AD6B1060DFE30131131768A86D17958E.description: Apply and extend previous understandings of multiplication and division to divide fractions by fractions.

AD6A8A10DFE30131131568A86D17958E.description: Use ratio reasoning to convert measurement units; manipulate and transform units appropriately when multiplying or dividing quantities.

AD6A4220DFE30131131468A86D17958E.description: Find a percent of a quantity as a rate per 100 (e.g., 30% of a quantity means 30/100 times the quantity); solve problems involving finding the whole, given a part and the percent.

comments: For example, if it took 7 hours to mow 4 lawns, then at that rate, how many lawns could be mowed in 35 hours? At what rate were lawns being mowed?
AD69EEA0DFE30131131368A86D17958E.description: Solve unit rate problems including those involving unit pricing and constant speed.

AD69A940DFE30131131268A86D17958E.description: Make tables of equivalent ratios relating quantities with whole number measurements, find missing values in the tables, and plot the pairs of values on the coordinate plane. Use tables to compare ratios.

AD696320DFE30131131168A86D17958E.description: Use ratio and rate reasoning to solve real-world and mathematical problems, e.g., by reasoning about tables of equivalent ratios, tape diagrams, double number line diagrams, or equations.

AD691AB0DFE30131131068A86D17958E.description: Understand the concept of a unit rate a/b associated with a ratio a:b with b ≠ 0, and use rate language in the context of a ratio relationship.
comments: Expectations for unit rates in this grade are limited to non-complex fractions.
Example: "This recipe has a ratio of 3 cups of flour to 4 cups of sugar, so there is 3/4 cup of flour for each cup of sugar." "We paid $75 for 15 hamburgers, which is a rate of $5 per hamburger."

Example: "The ratio of wings to beaks in the bird house at the zoo was 2:1, because for every 2 wings there was 1 beak." "For every vote candidate A received, candidate C received nearly three votes."
AD68D390DFE30131130F68A86D17958E.description: Understand the concept of a ratio and use ratio language to describe a ratio relationship between two quantities.

AD688D90DFE30131130E68A86D17958E.description: Understand ratio concepts and use ratio reasoning to solve problems.

AD67E530DFE30131130C68A86D17958E.description: Represent three-dimensional figures using nets made up of rectangles and triangles, and use the nets to find the surface area of these figures. Apply these techniques in the context of solving real-world and mathematical problems.

AD67A1C0DFE30131130B68A86D17958E.description: Draw polygons in the coordinate plane given coordinates for the vertices; use coordinates to find the length of a side joining points with the same first coordinate or the same second coordinate. Apply these techniques in the context of solving real-world and mathematical problems.

AD675D20DFE30131130A68A86D17958E.description: Find the volume of a right rectangular prism with fractional edge lengths by packing it with unit cubes of the appropriate unit fraction edge lengths, and show that the volume is the same as would be found by multiplying the edge lengths of the prism. Apply the formulas V = l w h and V = b h to find volumes of right rectangular prisms with fractional edge lengths in the context of solving real-world and mathematical problems.

AD671890DFE30131130968A86D17958E.description: Find the area of right triangles, other triangles, special quadrilaterals, and polygons by composing into rectangles or decomposing into triangles and other shapes; apply these techniques in the context of solving real-world and mathematical problems.

AD66D460DFE30131130868A86D17958E.description: Solve real-world and mathematical problems involving area, surface area, and volume.

AD663C30DFE30131130668A86D17958E.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.
comments: Mathematically proficient students notice if calculations are repeated, and look both for general methods and for shortcuts. Upper elementary students might notice when dividing 25 by 11 that they are repeating the same calculations over and over again, and conclude they have a repeating decimal. By paying attention to the calculation of slope as they repeatedly check whether points are on the line through (1, 2) with slope 3, middle school students might abstract the equation (y – 2)/(x – 1) = 3. Noticing the regularity in the way terms cancel when expanding (x – 1)(x + 1), (x – 1)(x² + x + 1), and (x – 1)(x³ + x² + x + 1) might lead them to the general formula for the sum of a geometric series. As they work to solve a problem, mathematically proficient students maintain oversight of the process, while attending to the details. They continually evaluate the reasonableness of their intermediate results.

Mathematically proficient students look closely to discern a pattern or structure. Young students, for example, might notice that three and seven more is the same amount as seven and three more, or they may sort a collection of shapes according to how many sides the shapes have. Later, students will see 7 × 8 equals the well remembered 7 × 5 + 7 × 3, in preparation for learning about the distributive property. In the expression x² + 9x + 14, older students can see the 14 as 2 × 7 and the 9 as 2 + 7. They recognize the significance of an existing line in a geometric figure and can use the strategy of drawing an auxiliary line for solving problems. They also can step back for an overview and shift perspective. They can see complicated things, such as some algebraic expressions, as single objects or as being composed of several objects. For example, they can see 5 – 3(x – y)² as 5 minus a positive number times a square and use that to realize that its value cannot be more than 5 for any real numbers x and y.
AD43DF80DFE30131130568A86D17958E.description: Look for and make use of structure.

comments: Mathematically proficient students try to communicate precisely to others. They try to use clear definitions in discussion with others and in their own reasoning. They state the meaning of the symbols they choose, including using the equal sign consistently and appropriately. They are careful about specifying units of measure, and labeling axes to clarify the correspondence with quantities in a problem. They calculate accurately and efficiently, express numerical answers with a degree of precision appropriate for the problem context. In the elementary grades, students give carefully formulated explanations to each other. By the time they reach high school they have learned to examine claims and make explicit use of definitions.

Mathematically proficient students consider the available tools when solving a mathematical problem. These tools might include pencil and paper, concrete models, a ruler, a protractor, a calculator, a spreadsheet, a computer algebra system, a statistical package, or dynamic geometry software. Proficient students are sufficiently familiar with tools appropriate for their grade or course to make sound decisions about when each of these tools might be helpful, recognizing both the insight to be gained and their limitations. For example, mathematically proficient high school students analyze graphs of functions and solutions generated using a graphing calculator. They detect possible errors by strategically using estimation and other mathematical knowledge. When making mathematical models, they know that technology can enable them to visualize the results of varying assumptions, explore consequences, and compare predictions with data. Mathematically proficient students at various grade levels are able to identify relevant external mathematical resources, such as digital content located on a website, and use them to pose or solve problems. They are able to use technological tools to explore and deepen their understanding of concepts.

Mathematically proficient students can apply the mathematics they know to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace. In early grades, this might be as simple as writing an addition equation to describe a situation. In middle grades, a student might apply proportional reasoning to plan a school event or analyze a problem in the community. By high school, a student might use geometry to solve a design problem or use a function to describe how one quantity of interest depends on another. Mathematically proficient students who can apply what they know are comfortable making assumptions and approximations to simplify a complicated situation, realizing that these may need revision later. They are able to identify important quantities in a practical situation and map their relationships using such tools as diagrams, two-way tables, graphs, flowcharts and formulas. They can analyze those relationships mathematically to draw conclusions. They routinely interpret their mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model if it has not served its purpose.

AD42A0D0DFE30131130168A86D17958E.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.
comments: Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases, and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and—if there is a flaw in an argument—explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.

Mathematically proficient students make sense of quantities and their relationships in problem situations. They bring two complementary abilities to bear on problems involving quantitative relationships: the ability to decontextualize—to abstract a given situation and represent it symbolically and manipulate the representing symbols as if they have a life of their own, without necessarily attending to their referents—and the ability to contextualize, to pause as needed during the manipulation process in order to probe into the referents for the symbols involved. Quantitative reasoning entails habits of creating a coherent representation of the problem at hand; considering the units involved; attending to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute them; and knowing and flexibly using different properties of operations and objects.

Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. Older students might, depending on the context of the problem, transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on their graphing calculator to get the information they need. Mathematically proficient students can explain correspondences between equations, verbal descriptions, tables, and graphs or draw diagrams of important features and relationships, graph data, and search for regularity or trends. Younger students might rely on using concrete objects or pictures to help conceptualize and solve a problem. Mathematically proficient students check their answers to problems using a different method, and they continually ask themselves, "Does this make sense?" They can understand the approaches of others to solving complex problems and identify correspondences between different approaches.
AD41E060DFE3013112FF68A86D17958E.description: Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them.

comments: Analytical Mathematics is a course designed for students who have successfully completed the Algebra II With Trigonometry course. It is considered to be parallel in rigor to Precalculus. This course provides a structured introduction to important areas of emphasis in most postsecondary studies that pursue a concentration in mathematics. Linear algebra, logic, vectors, and matrices are topics that are given more in-depth coverage than in previous courses. Application-based problem solving is an integral part of this course. To assist students with numerical and graphical analysis, the use of advanced technological tools is highly recommended.

While this course may be taken either prior to or after Precalculus, it is recommended that students who are interested in postsecondary studies in engineering successfully complete the Precalculus course as well as, where available, an Advanced Placement or International Baccalaureate calculus course.

comments: Precalculus is a course designed for students who have successfully completed the Algebra II With Trigonometry course. This course is considered to be a prerequisite for success in calculus and college mathematics. Algebraic, graphical, numerical, and verbal analyses are incorporated during investigations of the Precalculus content standards. Parametric equations, polar relations, vector operations, and limits are introduced. Content for this course also includes an expanded study of polynomial and rational functions, conic sections, trigonometric functions, and logarithmic and exponential functions.

Application-based problem solving is an integral part of the course. Instruction should include appropriate use of technology to facilitate continued development of students' higher-order thinking skills.

comments: Mathematical Investigations is a course designed for students who have successfully completed the Algebra II With Trigonometry course and who choose not to continue mathematics study in the Precalculus or Analytical Mathematics courses. This course may be offered as an elective for students who have completed the four mathematics requirements for graduation.

Mathematical Investigations is intended to extend students' knowledge of mathematical development. Beginning with ancient numeration systems, students explore relationships between mathematics and nature, music, art, and architecture as well as the contributions of well-known mathematicians. It extends the scope of prerequisite courses, integrating topics with an emphasis on application-based problem solving. The wide range of topics and applied problems may lend itself to organizing the content into thematic units. The prerequisites for this course are Algebra I, Geometry, and Algebra II With Trigonometry.

comments: The Algebra I course builds on foundational mathematics content learned by students in Grades K-8 by expanding mathematics understanding to provide students with a strong mathematics education. Content is designed to engage students in a variety of mathematical experiences that include the use of reasoning and problem-solving skills, which may be applied to life situations beyond the classroom setting. This course serves as the cornerstone for all high school mathematics courses; therefore, all subsequent mathematics courses require student mastery of the Algebra I content standards.

In contrast to the Algebra II With Trigonometry course, Algebra II does not meet the graduation requirements for the Alabama High School Diploma with Advanced Academic Endorsement due to the fact that it does not contain trigonometry content. Algebra II With Trigonometry or Algebra II is required to complete the graduation requirements for the Alabama High School Diploma. This course does not provide sufficient background to prepare students to pursue higher-level mathematics courses. The prerequisites for Algebra II are Algebra I and Geometry.

The star symbol sometimes appears on the heading for a group of standards; in that case, it should be understood to apply to all standards in that group.

ADFC32B0DFE3013113D668A86D17958E.description: Explain why the sum or product of two rational numbers is rational; that the sum of a rational number and an irrational number is irrational; and that the product of a nonzero rational number and an irrational number is irrational.

ADFBBC40DFE3013113D568A86D17958E.description: Use properties of rational and irrational numbers.
