comments: Example: creating a dance depicting happiness or anger

A044F290DFE30131FE3E68A86D17958E.description: Describe feelings, ideas, or images found in dance movements.
comments: Example: recognizing emotions in Baloo's dances in the movie The Jungle Book

A04475D0DFE30131FE3C68A86D17958E.description: Demonstrating basic nonlocomotor skills, including bending and stretching

A0443740DFE30131FE3B68A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate basic locomotor skills, including galloping, sliding, running, and walking

document.title: Alabama Course of Study: Science

0C533234848349A293528A87B494CA44.description: Evaluate a design solution (e.g., flood barriers, wind resistant roofs, lightning rods) that reduces the impact of a weather-related hazard.

2EF711A15157407EB99792B6854054D2.description: Collect information from a variety of sources to describe climates in different regions of the world.

B98EEFD52725468D936CFB444A9E9274.description: Display data graphically and in tables to describe typical weather conditions expected during a particular season (e.g., average temperature, precipitation, wind direction).

F185FA3ED88A477DA44AD07F793E494F.description: Evaluate engineered solutions to a problem created by environmental changes and any resulting impacts on the types and density of plant and animal populations living in the environment (e.g., replanting of sea oats in coastal areas due to destruction by hurricanes, creating property development restrictions in vacation areas to reduce displacement and loss of native animal populations).

EA6BDF695FF64553AB8B6CF44D0358E8.description: Categorize resources in various habitats as basic materials (e.g., sunlight, air, freshwater, soil), produced materials (e.g., food, fuel, shelter), or as nonmaterial (e.g., safety, instinct, nature-learned behaviors).

922EE4984B8848779CF263E279B11691.description: Create models that illustrate how organisms and their habitats make up a system in which the parts depend on each other.

BED0A460A46742D2A9A06915354AFFBD.description: Construct explanations that forming groups helps some organisms survive.

5C73150ACBF743228331FF23B8A486E2.description: Construct an argument from evidence to explain the likelihood of an organism's ability to survive when compared to the resources in a certain habitat (e.g., freshwater organisms survive well, less well, or not at all in saltwater; desert organisms survive well, less well, or not at all in woodlands).

AD93EF098DB84D0C9E415C162D68AB26.description: Investigate how variations in characteristics among individuals of the same species may provide advantages in surviving, finding mates, and reproducing (e.g., plants having larger thorns being less likely to be eaten by predators, animals having better camouflage coloration being more likely to survive and bear offspring).

E7620F63C9984B7D9FCB59411F164DE8.description: Analyze and interpret data from fossils (e.g., type, size, distribution) to provide evidence of organisms and the environments in which they lived long ago (e.g., marine fossils on dry land, tropical plant fossils in arctic areas, fossils of extinct organisms in any environment).

A10062C062224A6CB8275E491143C1D3.description: Engage in argument from evidence to justify that traits can be influenced by the environment (e.g., stunted growth in normally tall plants due to insufficient water, change in an arctic fox's fur color due to light and/or temperature, stunted growth of a normally large animal due to malnourishment).

C97FC3E785F846128F705AE9752495DC.description: Examine data to provide evidence that plants and animals, excluding humans, have traits inherited from parents and that variations of these traits exist in groups of similar organisms (e.g., flower colors in pea plants, fur color and pattern in animal offspring).

5D528AAAB27344F5B63E3BA78225F3C0.description: Heredity: Inheritance and Variation of Traits

E34268FD07424DE1B7BB31427BB7C8BB.description: Create representations to explain the unique and diverse life cycles of organisms other than humans (e.g., flowering plants, frogs, butterflies), including commonalities such as birth, growth, reproduction, and death.

098D7CC6B7D54766B5EE0C6CB9A0B718.description: Obtain and combine information to describe that organisms are classified as living things, rather than nonliving things, based on their ability to obtain and use resources, grow, reproduce, and maintain stable internal conditions while living in a constantly changing external environment.

F8E185105B0D4C95BE653271CDAB4D59.description: From Molecules to Organisms: Structures and Processes

14FEBCDD181C4EE78C614498FAC954E0.description: Apply scientific ideas about magnets to solve a problem through an engineering design project (e.g., constructing a latch to keep a door shut, creating a device to keep two moving objects from touching each other such as a maglev system).

BF5F6DB7E37B49199882254333999682.description: Explore objects that can be manipulated in order to determine cause-and-effect relationships (e.g., distance between objects affecting strength of a force, orientation of magnets affecting direction of a magnetic force) of electric interactions between two objects not in contact with one another (e.g., force on hair from an electrically charged balloon, electrical forces between a charged rod and pieces of paper) or magnetic interactions between two objects not in contact with one another (e.g., force between two permanent magnets or between an electromagnet and steel paperclips, force exerted by one magnet versus the force exerted by two magnets).

C730BC11E62A4E04B98058D47B813A64.description: Investigate, measure, and communicate in a graphical format how an observed pattern of motion (e.g., a child swinging in a swing, a ball rolling back and forth in a bowl, two children teetering on a see-saw, a model vehicle rolling down a ramp of varying heights, a pendulum swinging) can be used to predict the future motion of an object.

36F6724AA122469B89ED7BB5FF9F5706.description: Plan and carry out an experiment to determine the effects of balanced and unbalanced forces on the motion of an object using one variable at a time, including number, size, direction, speed, position, friction, or air resistance (e.g., balanced forces pushing from both sides on an object, such as a box, producing no motion; unbalanced force on one side of an object, such as a ball, producing motion), and communicate these findings graphically.

3C9E5D8FB90C41F9AE1464098F2660B0.description: Motion and Stability: Forces and Interactions

document.title: Alabama Course of Study: Science

A491E3CE0ED7454FB328967F5E3E6DCA.description: Formulate and evaluate solutions to limit the effects of natural Earth processes on humans (e.g., designing earthquake, tornado, or hurricane-resistant buildings; improving monitoring of volcanic activity).

4A7BBD48A06D46AF965889941E854011.description: Describe patterns of Earth's features on land and in the ocean using data from maps (e.g., topographic maps of Earth's land and ocean floor; maps of locations of mountains, continental boundaries, volcanoes, and earthquakes).

1B5D1CED748541B69F4AB8E84FD69E4A.description: Analyze and interpret data (e.g., angle of slope in downhill movement of water, volume of water flow, cycles of freezing and thawing of water, cycles of heating and cooling of water, speed of wind, relative rate of soil deposition, amount of vegetation) to determine effects of weathering and rate of erosion by water, ice, wind, and vegetation using one single form of weathering or erosion at a time.

8CAC9A7BFB6244ACB19C2342D9C625ED.description: Explore information to support the claim that landforms are the result of a combination of constructive forces, including crustal deformation, volcanic eruptions, and sediment deposition as well as a result of destructive forces, including erosion and weathering.

D32BEE9FFD0E4AC298123C5F10B70C7E.description: Plan and carry out investigations to examine properties of soils and soil types (e.g., color, texture, capacity to retain water, ability to support growth of plants).

6BEA5AC9626948299EFFEB58424340C3.description: Construct explanations by citing evidence found in patterns of rock formations and fossils in rock layers that Earth changes over time through both slow and rapid processes (e.g., rock layers containing shell fossils appearing above rock layers containing plant fossils and no shells indicating a change from land to water over time, a canyon with different rock layers in the walls and a river in the bottom indicating that over time a river cut through the rock).

65DE70B00AC64224AE58093B11B59122.description: Investigate different ways animals receive information through the senses, process that information, and respond to it in different ways (e.g., skunks lifting tails and spraying an odor when threatened, dogs moving ears when reacting to sound, snakes coiling or striking when sensing vibrations).

C1ED056268F1426AACCF9519DD16DB9D.description: Obtain and communicate information explaining that humans have systems that interact with one another for digestion, respiration, circulation, excretion, movement, control, coordination, and protection from disease.

DD22197D04DA430E85465C99CACE1A30.description: Examine evidence to support an argument that the internal and external structures of plants (e.g., thorns, leaves, stems, roots, colored petals, xylem, phloem) and animals (e.g., heart, stomach, lung, brain, skin) function to support survival, growth, behavior, and reproduction.

07E2F9D3E72D489F87EEBE92EEDAFA73.description: From Molecules to Organisms: Structures and Processes

5D33AFF85AB44EB796845DCB4BDD4259.description: Construct a model to explain that an object can be seen when light reflected from its surface enters the eyes.

21BD1AB031EB4314B84F091B716DA74D.description: Develop and use models to show multiple solutions in which patterns are used to transfer information (e.g., using a grid of 1s and 0s representing black and white to send information about a picture, using drums to send coded information through sound waves, using Morse code to send a message).

931C756E06994A51B450D189E3E67AF6.description: Develop a model of waves to describe patterns in terms of amplitude and wavelength, and including that waves can cause objects to move.

9F5CD28054DF409EAE222D0796131504.description: Waves and Their Applications in Technologies for Information Transfer

A62DDBFE89064BF18CE85221E96577A5.description: Compile information to describe how the use of energy derived from natural renewable and nonrenewable resources affects the environment (e.g., constructing dams to harness energy from water, a renewable resource, while causing a loss of animal habitats; burning of fossil fuels, a nonrenewable resource, while causing an increase in air pollution; installing solar panels to harness energy from the sun, a renewable resource, while requiring specialized materials that necessitate mining).

83717F9F18464FE6910B2D7F01857B71.description: Design, construct, and test a device that changes energy from one form to another (e.g., electric circuits converting electrical energy into motion, light, or sound energy; a passive solar heater converting light energy into heat energy).

4B15B9C378484312A8C95B746A916771.description: Investigate to determine changes in energy resulting from increases or decreases in speed that occur when objects collide.

964D1C283B704001B679B93530A2EE30.description: Demonstrate that electric circuits require a complete loop through which an electric current can pass.

12BB9018D0C648B0AAA596A5B4D64C61.description: Demonstrate that different objects can absorb, reflect, and/or conduct energy.

E4EBD11F20584833BB17A4EAB6BDFFDF.description: Provide evidence that heat can be produced in many ways (e.g., rubbing hands together, burning leaves) and can move from one object to another by conduction.

EC4F6DDA72B74751805CE98B2940C766.description: Plan and carry out investigations that explain transference of energy from place to place by sound, light, heat, and electric currents.

1B2FA985DC4A4AE3B6BDE40160239AC4.description: Use evidence to explain the relationship of the speed of an object to the energy of that object.

document.title: Alabama Course of Study: Science

866E11DE90054A0B8E845FE604A01534.description: Construct an explanation from evidence that natural selection acting over generations may lead to the predominance of certain traits that support successful survival and reproduction of a population and to the suppression of other traits.

686288F70DEB4037A1B52138079A6131.description: Obtain and evaluate pictorial data to compare patterns in the embryological development across multiple species to identify relationships not evident in the adult anatomy.

7AE331537C584D87A4821D3BC6C1CC47.description: Construct an explanation based on evidence (e.g., cladogram, phylogenetic tree) for the anatomical similarities and differences among modern organisms and between modern and fossil organisms, including living fossils (e.g., alligator, horseshoe crab, nautilus, coelacanth).

6165F5A0470E4E64AB5FBC9E02E4218B.description: Analyze and interpret data for patterns of change in anatomical structures of organisms using the fossil record and the chronological order of fossil appearance in rock layers.

83972E67D03145CFAA988A7A313BF254.description: Gather and synthesize information regarding the impact of technologies (e.g., hand pollination, selective breeding, genetic engineering, genetic modification, gene therapy) on the inheritance and/or appearance of desired traits in organism.

FFF658E34DA24D499B238C9310CEE0AA.description: Construct an explanation from evidence to describe how genetic mutations result in harmful, beneficial, or neutral effects to the structure and function of an organism.

A70C3F916E114571A506C742A2ED811D.description: Construct and use models (e.g., monohybrid crosses using Punnett squares, diagrams, simulations) to explain that genetic variations between parent and offspring (e.g., different alleles, mutations) occur as a result of genetic differences in randomly inherited genes located on chromosomes and that additional variations may arise from alteration of genetic information.

2D64E59F307D4F7DBD58CD2CDC2C3C06.description: Heredity: Inheritance and Variation of Traits

829DBCF42D9242C6A6726ED54B3A5BF6.description: Analyze and interpret data to predict how environmental conditions (e.g., weather, availability of nutrients, location) and genetic factors (e.g., selective breeding of cattle or crops) influence the growth of organisms (e.g., drought decreasing plant growth, adequate supply of nutrients for maintaining normal plant growth, identical plant seeds growing at different rates in different weather conditions, fish growing larger in large ponds than in small ponds).

081FCA78D8D5457AA72BFDD5ECD805C9.description: Use evidence and scientific reasoning to explain how characteristic animal behaviors (e.g., building nests to protect young from cold, herding to protect young from predators, attracting mates for breeding by producing special sounds and displaying colorful plumage, transferring pollen or seeds to create conditions for seed germination and growth) and specialized plant structures (e.g., flower brightness, nectar, and odor attracting birds that transfer pollen; hard outer shells on seeds providing protection prior to germination) affect the probability of successful reproduction of both animals and plants.

8F30083F006D4A7682DA12802B95A772.description: Engage in argument to defend the effectiveness of a design solution that maintains biodiversity and ecosystem services (e.g., using scientific, economic, and social considerations regarding purifying water, recycling nutrients, preventing soil erosion).

D5868CB66EF540BD9EE95FFEE1A034E8.description: Construct an explanation to predict patterns of interactions in different ecosystems in terms of the relationships between and among organisms (e.g., competition, predation, mutualism, commensalism, parasitism).

FEF6B078CB4842FA8E5F758B3F40E461.description: Use empirical evidence from patterns and data to demonstrate how changes to physical or biological components of an ecosystem (e.g., deforestation, succession, drought, fire, disease, human activities, invasive species) can lead to shifts in populations.

F7407E4F1FF3466883DC28A93F6559FA.description: Analyze and interpret data to provide evidence regarding how resource availability impacts individual organisms as well as populations of organisms within an ecosystem.

4D167AF9CC4F4DA79778087FC3E709CF.description: Generate a scientific explanation based on evidence for the role of photosynthesis and cellular respiration in the cycling of matter and flow of energy into and out of organisms.

470A0D35CEB54528848D87405C0FFF1C.description: Obtain, evaluate, and communicate information about how food is broken down through chemical reactions to create new molecules that support growth and/or release energy as it moves through an organism.

61D7B7394E8249C395702E193EB1727A.description: Examine the cycling of matter between abiotic and biotic parts of ecosystems to explain the flow of energy and the conservation of matter.

2931A5C599E34B47A9F73E0EFC2F8FEB.description: Construct models and representations of organ systems (e.g., circulatory, digestive, respiratory, muscular, skeletal, nervous) to demonstrate how multiple interacting organs and systems work together to accomplish specific functions.

E1FA2A635D4D45BE99979805513A1FE4.description: Construct an explanation of the function (e.g., mitochondria releasing energy during cellular respiration) of specific cell structures (i.e., nucleus, cell membrane, cell wall, ribosomes, mitochondria, chloroplasts, and vacuoles) for maintaining a stable environment.

37E5E8B8E9FD4354B551EE3C01C56918.description: Gather and synthesize information to explain how prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells differ in structure and function, including the methods of asexual and sexual reproduction.

BE7D5E14B1464813A4713F426258E85A.description: Engage in argument from evidence to support claims of the cell theory.

26774A00CB704ADEB4FE0BFBDF9F397A.description: From Molecules to Organisms: Structures and Processes

document.title: Alabama Course of Study: Arts Education Visual Arts

A375E420DFE3013102C668A86D17958E.description: Identify works of art from various artists that were inspired by the environments in which they were created.
comments: Example: Alabama artists inspired by their heritage and environment, including Howard Finster's painting Coke Bottle, Jimmy Lee Sudduth's painting Cotton Pickers, and Frank Fleming's sculpture Storyteller

A375A8B0DFE3013102C568A86D17958E.description: Utilize community resources to identify works of art from various cultures, times, and places.
comments: Examples: guest artists, artists-in-residence, museums, libraries, universities

A3753260DFE3013102C368A86D17958E.description: Compare different interpretations of the same subject or theme in art.
comments: Example: landscapes by Impressionist and Hudson River School artists

A374F470DFE3013102C268A86D17958E.description: Describe functions of art within the total environment, including functional sculptures, urban improvement, and transportation.
comments: Examples: functional sculptures—fountains, benches, playground equipment; urban improvement—murals on walls; transportation—bridges

A374B2E0DFE3013102C168A86D17958E.description: Critiquing works of art orally or in writing, using the elements of art and principles of design
comments: Example: reflecting upon the creative process and success of personal works of art in an electronic portfolio

A37462A0DFE3013102C068A86D17958E.description: Describe how the elements of art and principles of design, including rhythm, movement, and emphasis, are used in a specific work of art.
comments: Examples: movement as depicted in the use of line and painting techniques in Wassily Kandinsky's abstract works, emphasis as depicted in Giorgio de Chirico's The Nostalgia of the Infinite, rhythm as depicted in Jackson Pollock's Autumn Rhythm, movement in Glenna Goodacre's sculpture Puddle Jumpers

A373CD90DFE3013102BE68A86D17958E.description: Apply the elements of art and principles of design, including rhythm, movement, and emphasis, in the creation of works of art.
comments: Examples: producing collages or paintings similar to those of Romare Bearden and Piet Mondrian that were inspired by music, creating works of art similar to Diego Rivera's works that were inspired by everyday life experiences in Mexico

A3738440DFE3013102BD68A86D17958E.description: Use traditional and digital media in the production of graphic design to communicate ideas and feelings.
comments: Example: designing posters, book covers, or logos on the themes of recycling, drug awareness, or endangered species

A3733600DFE3013102BC68A86D17958E.description: Produce two- and three-dimensional works of art with a variety of traditional and digital processes, materials, subject matter, and techniques.
comments:
Examples: processes—using a digital camera to create images to be digitally altered;
materials—creating papier-mâché animals;
subject matter—creating portraits, landscapes, still lifes, interiors, or seascapes;
techniques—layering materials such as cardboard, rubber, fabric, paper clips, and papers to create a collagraph

document.title: Alabama Course of Study: Health Education

A4561180DFE30131044368A86D17958E.description: Describe risk factors that can lead to substance abuse.
comments: Examples: peer pressure, family history, stress, depression, psychological disorders

A455D1F0DFE30131044268A86D17958E.description: Describe physical effects of substance abuse on the body.
comments: Examples: shortness of breath, elevated heart rate, stained teeth, impaired judgment, addiction

A45527E0DFE30131044068A86D17958E.description: Differentiate between acute and chronic medical conditions.
comments: Examples: acute—flu, strep throat chronic—asthma, diabetes
Example: following recommended cleaning, cooking, and storing practices

A4541F30DFE30131043C68A86D17958E.description: Describing how media, culture, and availability influence food choices

A453A2B0DFE30131043A68A86D17958E.description: Explain relationships among nutrition, health, and wellness.
comments: Examples: impact of following national dietary guidelines, long-term effects of eating saturated fats, risks of excessive sugar and caffeine intake

A4545B00DFE30131043D68A86D17958E.description: Utilize information on food labels to determine the nutritional value of various foods

comments: Examples: responding to nonverbal cues, tolerating opinions, recognizing personal space
A45311F0DFE30131043868A86D17958E.description: Identify ways to respect personal boundaries of others.

A452D200DFE30131043768A86D17958E.description: Describe healthful ways to express emotions.
comments: Examples: journaling, talking to an older sibling or trusted adult

A4525850DFE30131043568A86D17958E.description: Describe the importance of personal hygiene health habits related to puberty and adolescence.

A4521B10DFE30131043468A86D17958E.description: Identify benefits of adequate sleep, nutrition, and exercise for the body.
comments: Examples: mental alertness, strong immune system, healthy weight

A45197C0DFE30131043268A86D17958E.description: Explain the importance of communication within the family unit.

A450FEE0DFE30131043068A86D17958E.description: Identify environmental health issues related to home and work.
comments: Examples: waste disposal, stagnant water, mold

A450C010DFE30131042F68A86D17958E.description: Explain ways industry impacts environmental and community health.
comments: Examples: land, air, noise, or water pollution; disposal of hazardous waste

9F1EA57205664F13BA9DEA3EABBBD370.description: Use mathematical equations (e.g., (m<sub>1</sub>v<sub>1</sub> + m<sub>2</sub>v<sub>2</sub>)<sub>before</sub> = (m<sub>1</sub>v<sub>1</sub> + m<sub>2</sub>v<sub>2</sub>)<sub>after</sub>) and diagrams to explain that the total momentum of a system of objects is conserved when there is no net external force on the system.

0991CEF38CFE4DC2B30AEBEE6905FF83.description: Apply Newton's laws to predict the motion of a system by constructing force diagrams that identify the external forces acting on the system, including friction (e.g., a book on a table, an object being pushed across a floor, an accelerating car).

6A921C0CF8114ACCA2B712E71AD6EFE2.description: Analyze and interpret data for one- and two-dimensional motion applying basic concepts of distance, displacement, speed, velocity, and acceleration (e.g., velocity versus time graphs, displacement versus time graphs, acceleration versus time graphs).

7AB5BF68D027491494F58EDB37484094.description: Motion and Stability: Forces and Interactions

3F86568EEF5444DF8994CDB1CF616A29.description: Develop arguments for and against nuclear power generation compared to other types of power generation.

390CE46670454C09B5FADD557D13361A.description: Research and communicate information about types of naturally occurring radiation and their properties.

B53CB2DD5CE043CEB0A5C6317E9CADCE.description: Develop models to illustrate the concept of half-life for radioactive decay.

F5C3E213EEF14525979842EC7F86C887.description: Use mathematical representations to support and verify the claim that atoms, and therefore mass, are conserved during a simple chemical reaction.

335B911C346B4629AA6BC858F6121A7C.description: Analyze and interpret data using acid-base indicators (e.g., color-changing markers, pH paper) to distinguish between acids and bases, including comparisons between strong and weak acids and bases.

1A1FDB7D68E64C9DBA422140B3DD7C2A.description: Analyze and interpret data from a simple chemical reaction or combustion reaction involving main group elements.

3851DB20CBEE425EA764514C295C5444.description: Plan and carry out investigations (e.g., squeezing a balloon, placing a balloon on ice) to identify the relationships that exist among the pressure, volume, density, and temperature of a confined gas.

C89243C5C5FF43CFBEB0301F6D5E5FC1.description: Use the periodic table as a model to predict the relative properties and trends (e.g., reactivity of metals; types of bonds formed, including ionic, covalent, and polar covalent; numbers of bonds formed; reactions with oxygen) of main group elements based on the patterns of valence electrons in atoms.

document.title: Alabama Course of Study: Languages Other Than English—Foreign Languages

2AA937DF57E242E68D99F2C4C7202F05.description: Use language skills and cultural knowledge for practical life applications.

09BE06B522094516B3FCBDEAC1503930.description: Describe similarities and differences that exist within a target culture.

53D2E6EC06AE45998EEC2B1AB46094D2.description: Compare the complex elements of the target language and English.

Example: "The Raven" and "Jabberwocky"
E05129153CAE45DBAA235F78DC2C66B5.description: Identifying interpreted poetry and its English equivalent.

50B23B2BC2E04B73B966849070318E6F.description: Identifying major deaf and hearing authors.

DC8F8068AB9D43819F8A50A0E5919634.description: Trace cultural developments of the target culture.
comments: Examples: expressive art forms, contemporary or historical issues

A0FAE78D62754BFA8D7796A5B6947D67.description: Relate the role of historic events to the development of the target culture.
comments: Examples: French influence on American Sign Language, Civil Rights Act and its influence on special education, debates of Alexander Graham Bell and Thomas Gallaudet regarding oral versus manual approach

A0467409A40843389487F244833469E9.description: Create original prose and poetry presentations in the target language using appropriate vocabulary and learned structures and time frames.
comments: Examples: stories, poems, dramatizations

5926B3BE6C5A47AEB951D9CB364F8A68.description: Interpret complex materials in the target language using learned structures and tenses.
comments: Examples: Interpreting humor, irony, simile, and metaphor in authentic prose and poetry selections

CD28C49E79D64BB5992BA0F903E63BB4.description: Apply the target language to support and defend opinions and preferences, to propose and support solutions to issues and problems, and to express needs and desires, including the use of circumlocution, body language, and other creative means to convey and comprehend messages in all time frames.

83458C0CF74C4C1D9FE69E28764383ED.description: Apply language skills and cultural knowledge to access information for recreational, educational, and occupational purposes.
comments: Examples: recreational—Deaf Olympics, sporting events; educational—National Technical Institute for the Deaf (NTID), Gallaudet University; occupational—Internet sites, job interviews

4E375CAB47C54C69BE0720E05A92EA50.description: Explain the origins of typical activities and events of the target culture community.
comments: Examples: political and historic events—"Deaf President Now," a 1988 week-long strike by Gallaudet students resulting in the appointment of a deaf president and restructuring of the Board of Regents

B404C00FE66848F3817346A6E800AC7B.description: Comparing aspects of target cultures, including language, values, and types of recreation

4700155CE0984EBCA573D2A96CE207E7.description: Comparing social conventions of target cultures

0B5E09A7D388433D8467A357488E3507.description: Describing influences of events and issues on the relationship between target cultures

2E136A7122444C5EAADF821C3B6006CD.description: Identify similarities and differences that exist within the American Sign Language culture and other Deaf cultures.

F1CDB5722ACD4362B7773B1B49E29AA7.description: Identifying examples that show how vocabulary, linguistic structures, and tense usage in the target language differ from those of English.
comments: Example: American Sign Language—TOUCH FINISH, NEW–YORK and English—I have been to New York.

EAEB55C10FFD4561AA2D5D806124BC84.description: Identifying examples of ways in which language and meaning do not transfer directly from one language to another.
comments: Examples: to be rarely used in American Sign Language, no written form of American Sign Language

comments: Examples: relative clauses, embedded clauses, spatial relationships

7AB0A35218BF472A90C02A220118FE85.description: Apply information learned in other school subject areas to information learned from target language materials.
comments: Examples: information on hazards and hearing loss in health education programs, advocacy awareness information learned in social studies programs, language literacy gained from English language arts programs

Examples: historic events—Milan Manifesto and the 1880 oral-only vote; political structures—influence on other countries of the Deaf Child Bill of Rights; economic factors—Deaf adults immigrating to the United States in search of career opportunities; artistic expressions—Deaf Way Conference at Gallaudet University where Deaf artists from around the world were first brought together to share their expertise
C26049BF218048DE80C780FF0265C266.description: Describe the global influences of historic events, political structures, economic factors, and artistic expressions of the target culture.

28AEE7A41FF44DBDB171063001C9084E.description: Analyze information learned about the perspectives and practices of the target culture to describe patterns of behavior typically associated with other target language cultures.

CB4122925A51425A98F9AEB33CFACDA0.description: Create presentations in the target language on a variety of topics using familiar and newly acquired vocabulary words and phrases and correct structure.
comments: Examples: advertisements, speeches, poems, ABC and classifier stories

04A363DC660E489DB8A50B5D5AFFE0C2.description: Identifying characters in relation to space and location

E95FCD397C5046759B1FF6A6B232CC5E.description: Identifying complex sentence structures and clauses.
comments: Example: rhetorical, conditional, and relative clauses

5BD64E88DE98492C8644FDC851E48C59.description: Interpret culturally authentic presentations in the target language about familiar and unfamiliar topics to determine main ideas and supporting details.

94F0277A834747D5942A857F7CCAB515.description: Use the target language, including exchanging ideas, restating or paraphrasing, explaining, and giving cause to interact in a variety of settings.
comments: Examples: dialogues, retells, impromptu role plays, articles on current events

1BA7545FC6504A94A465BAA039E69F31.description: Communicate in a variety of ways with speakers of the target language on topics of interest.
comments: Examples: writing letters and e-mail correspondence, conducting interviews
Examples: performances, sporting events, Deaf Club meetings, residential alumni meetings, pageants
A796F4130FC24C9AB1F228B97197F54D.description: Describe typical activities and events of the target language community.

21C74A28119A41BF9A17E989582CE615.description: Compare social interactions in a variety of cultural settings with those of the target culture.
comments: Examples: maintaining eye contact, pointing, hugging, touching

6D9AD891DD8940DB8F0AA2B4FC723498.description: Compare vocabulary usage, grammatical structures, and idiomatic expressions of the target language with other signed systems and with English.

D1372119F2AB4B4889E1D8537E25CB91.description: Relate information learned in other school subjects, including political issues, social issues, and educational concerns, to the target culture.
comments: Examples: political issues—Civil Rights Act, Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), public policy; social issues—oral-sign communication, cochlear implants; educational concerns—residential versus inclusion, Deaf Child Bill of Rights

32BC0B2F012C4546AE0BD807D029289B.description: Explain basic social, economic, and political institutions of the target culture.
comments: Examples: social—Deaf Clubs; economic—National Fraternal Society of the Deaf (NFSD); political—World Federation of the Deaf (WFD), National Association of the Deaf (NAD)
Examples: club events, sporting events, celebrations, traditions
CF1FDC138E2E42F8B141439944AEF282.description: Describe social practices within cultures where the target language is used.

561447EAA6A04EE18EA8F2B6BB2D0600.description: Recite from memory skits, poems, short narratives, or songs in the target language using appropriate spacing, basic classifiers, and nonmanual grammatical signals.

2CCA667030A14F35828D38748563E49E.description: Create short presentations in the target language on a variety of topics using familiar and newly acquired vocabulary words and phrases and correct syntax and grammar.
comments: Examples: skits, ABC stories, classifier stories, original poems, commercials
Examples: setting, plot, characters, conflict

8374EAACBFB5435FBC9219E9F12113A1.description: Identifying specific linguistic aspects of American Sign Language.
comments: Examples: lexicalized signs, multiple meanings, plurals, time indicators

4C3287C1278841BB9E3789F57660E70B.description: Interpret culturally authentic narratives in the target language about new and familiar topics.

D6FC3372FF4F4B24A07AB23D18429934.description: Use learned target language vocabulary and phrases, including giving and responding to a series of commands, asking and answering questions, providing directions and instructions, and stating preferences and opinions to interact in a variety of situations.

B75C92813CAD4A20BCFAA98A9519B84B.description: Identify situations and resources in which target language skills and cultural knowledge may be applied beyond the classroom setting.
comments: Examples: situations—need for interpreters in businesses, courts, hospitals, and performances; resources—print media, entertainment, technology

1828026299D64B9688620127EE64A62B.description: Identify typical cultural activities and events of the target language community.
comments: Examples: Deaf Awareness Day, sporting events, signed performances

1116372E023446F695A78190AE1C598F.description: Compare customs of the target culture to those of other minority deaf cultures, including celebrations and traditions.
comments: Examples: celebrations—Gallaudet Day and Deaf Awareness Day in the United States and "Learn to Sign Week" in England; traditions—greater number of residential schools in the United States, differences in sporting events, greater number of Deaf Club memberships in other countries

C21164F0DA0B4457BA3310C57F5B80BA.description: Identify similarities and differences between signed words and phrases and their parameters, including hand shape, palm orientation, movement, location, and nonmanual grammatical signals.

8CA3709D7E9243199CA4E5F383608701.description: Identify information common to other school subjects and the target language community, including history, the arts, physical education, and science.
comments: Examples: history—settlement of Martha's Vineyard; arts—Douglas Tilden, National Theater for the Deaf, Henry Kisor; physical education—creation of the huddle, umpire signals; science—deaf and hard of hearing scientists and their scientific works

A5F8CC9C26AF4F01B89E33A15C3F5184.description: Identify tangible and intangible products of a target culture, including symbols and expressive art forms.
comments: Examples: tangible—teletypewriter for the Deaf (TTY), videophone, signaling devices; intangible—ABC stories, literature, relay services

536688961C7C4A3380D7EEEA269E2D59.description: Use appropriate nonverbal behavior in a variety of social situations and familiar settings.
comments: Examples: personal space, hugging, eye contact, signals for gaining attention, nonmanual grammatical signals

4832134C19D2405698F5521AECF9D762.description: Read aloud proverbs, short poems, and songs in the target language using appropriate syntax and grammar, facial expression, and body movement.

A0476EA809C947328A64BA93105DEF59.description: Create brief presentations in the target language about everyday topics using familiar and newly acquired vocabulary words and phrases and correct structure in the present time frame.
comments: Examples: short autobiographies, descriptions of daily and leisure activities

E8E25A9F6ED64C5A8DA341FD0BE65520.description: Identify main ideas and designated facts from signed narratives about familiar topics presented in the present time frame.

DD8D9C024B074A4690F2F6D056BF0261.description: Responding to basic instructions and questions

87228547CC66459F95B9F776A8ADE4DC.description: Recognize basic physical and linguistic features of the target language used in common words and phrases.
comments: Examples: physical features—nonmanual grammatical signals, hand dominance, parameters, body movement; linguistic features—classifiers; nouns versus verbs; temporal aspect; basic sentences involving negation, questions, and comments

C7561E134F6A425D873DD3E49C266047.description: Use the target language in the present time frame, including salutations, farewells, expressions of courtesy, likes, dislikes, feelings, emotions, agreement, disagreement, requests, descriptions, sequenced information, and cultural references where appropriate to interact in a variety of situations.

FC82B2D4F99F47E6B6FA5396E98E71E1.description: Identify English derivatives of Latin words commonly used in Latin poetry.
comments: Examples: urbane, amorous, incantation, Occident
Example: themes of love and hate in different versions of Catullus' "Odi et amo" and works by English poets Abraham Cowley (1667), Ezra Pound (1972), and Gary Wills (contemporary)
E845C41B4CA2493EA671C321B9C67DD6.description: Compare universal themes found in Roman poetry to artistic renditions of other time periods and cultures.

27E8FC03D4BD46A984EAF6F0E3E0532F.description: Identify phrases used in English and their origins in Latin literature.
comments: Examples: "vanish into thin air," "hair stands on end," and "voice sticks in your throat" originating in Vergil's The Aeneid
Example: Ovid's tale of Orpheus and Eurydice as interpreted in the modern Brazilian film Black Orpheus
F40FA97A4E3F4279BED261A753713EF6.description: Describe the influence of themes in Roman poetry on Western art and literature.

84494F51ED9D4548984C7BDD5F267057.description: Analyze Roman poets to determine their influence on art and literature throughout history.
comments: Example: Ovid's influence on Gianlorenzo Bernini's sculptural rendition of Daphne and Apollo, William Shakespeare's Romeo and Juliet, and Leonard Bernstein's West Side Story

22374107264343C6B6057B5DB98833B7.description: Compare actions and character traits of Roman heroes to actions and character traits of heroes of other periods in history.
comments: Examples: Vergil's Aeneas and George Washington, Ovid's Daedalus and Leonardo da Vinci

A19664725AEB4CBEBD64864F3243BD86.description: Explain the significance of Roman poets.
comments: Examples: Vergil, Horace, Ovid, Catullus, Martial, patron Maecenas

1FD22989B6024056A077A4BB44BC35E7.description: Describe Roman values and perspectives in poetry.
comments: Example: Epicurean and Stoic philosophies
Examples: Catullus' 5 ("Vivamus, mea Lesbia, atque amemus"), Horace's 1.11 ("Carpe Diem")

EA0C00E24893494DA83DCF222E6F2002.description: Identify metrical patterns by scanning selected Latin poetry.
comments: Example: dactylic hexameter in Vergil's The Aeneid—"Ārmă vĭr/ūmqŭe că/nō Trō/iāe quī/prīmŭs ăb/ōrīs"

250CA685CE7048EDA80B0D01242C4EA5.description: Analyze the style of Latin poets to comprehend content.
comments: Example: describing how the meter of a poem affects its meaning

528DE783FD964C2BA7369ACCFA71DB1F.description: Use Level IV Latin grammar and syntax to read original works by authors of Latin poetry.
comments: Examples: grammar and syntax—supine, diminutive, correlatives, enclitics, syncopated verb forms, impersonal verbs; rhetorical figures, including anaphora, hyperbole, chiasmus, polysyndeton, asyndeton, simile, litotes; perfect and pluperfect subjunctive, independent subjunctives, conditional sentences, subordinate subjunctive clauses, including cum clauses, anticipatory, fearing, indirect question, indirect command, substantive result clause, characteristic, relative result, proviso, clause of comparison, doubting, hindrance, subjunctive by attraction, subordinate clause in indirect statements; vocabulary learned in the dictionary format; authors of Latin poetry—Vergil, Ovid, Horace, Catullus

25C0E7B6A5A6458BA666C1D95FAD977C.description: Identify English derivatives of Latin words commonly used in Latin prose.
comments: Examples: avarice, vulgar, suspicion, perdition

CF961A638BC74FE8B99F6DF7FB9D0D7C.description: Compare issues that reveal cultural similarities between the ancient world and modern cultures.
comments: Examples: Sallust's account of the 63 B.C. senate debate on capital punishment and the modern debate on capital punishment, Cicero's consternation regarding the appropriate punishment of insurgent citizens and the current debate on the Patriot Act

3C01BAA505DB41ABA4FC474E6025EDF5.description: Compare the style of Roman prose authors to that used in contemporary history and politics.

1CD3066B3C9B4362A4DA974FEC7E1D07.description: Analyze the structure of Roman rhetoric and its influence on contemporary rhetorical styles.
comments: Example: comparing one of Cicero's orations to Martin Luther King's "I Have a Dream" speech

A02DF08A7E5D4DDBB1E6B87CF0897B04.description: Analyze selected Roman prose to describe its influence in today's world of diverse cultures.
comments: Example: use of phrases such as "O tempora, O mores" in modern context

81638E6C75964B548F20FC87AC92B884.description: Describe the influence of themes in Roman prose on Western art and literature.
comments: Example: Jacques-Louis David's Oath of the Horatii

5D435475868D4A6D8FD38044C1EB7B13.description: Analyze early Roman heroes to identify their influence on American history.
comments: Example: describing the influence of Cincinnatus on George Washington

A2C56BA5ECA148F896061333A32D6352.description: Contrast the ideals of Roman political factions in the first century B.C.
comments: Example: conflict between Cicero and Catiline
Examples: Cicero, Pliny the Elder, Pliny the Younger, Sallust, Catiline, Seneca, the Gracchi, Plautus, Terence, Livy, Tacitus
9291620A48A64677B7058043327012A3.description: Analyze figures in Roman history to determine their cultural significance.

A8C53EF3EB6A453D914A58440DF2DA3D.description: Describe Roman values and perspectives recorded in prose.
comments: Example: values of pietas and gravitas found in the writings of Pliny

7EB3B1E44B95419E9474A92F71AB4A3E.description: Analyze the style of Latin prose authors to comprehend content.
comments: Examples: describing the tone of a passage from Cicero, explaining the use of rhetorical devices in speeches by Cicero

D33436C1A64D4CD3B0654A5FF8EE9DC0.description: Use Level III Latin grammar and syntax to read original works by authors of Latin prose and to write Latin prose.
comments: Examples: grammar and syntax—supine, diminutive, correlatives, enclitics, syncopated verb forms, impersonal verbs; rhetorical figures, including anaphora, hyperbole, chiasmus, polysyndeton, asyndeton, simile, litotes; perfect and pluperfect subjunctive, independent subjunctives, conditional sentences, subordinate subjunctive clauses, including cum clauses, anticipatory, fearing, indirect question, indirect command, substantive result clause, characteristic, relative result, proviso, clause of comparison, doubting, hindrance, subjunctive by attraction, subordinate clause in indirect statements; vocabulary learned in the dictionary format; authors of Latin prose—Caesar, Cicero, Pliny, Sallust, Livy

1FBE491C93EA41DF9422457137E0F18D.description: Identify ways the study of Latin is beneficial to the study of other languages.
comments: Example: similarities among the Latin word homo, the Spanish word hombre, and the French word l'homme

5E541B225BCC4306A4943DC43A9F2C92.description: Compare the geography and social, political, legal, military, and economic systems of the Roman world to systems of the modern world.
comments: Example: comparing a map of the Roman Empire to a contemporary map of the world

EF34905EE3CB403587E62882A07FDB9A.description: Utilize Latin prefixes, suffixes, and roots to expand English vocabulary.
comments: Examples: recall, advocate, admit, absent

D018B059488B44088AAD8689F1A35DA6.description: Compare language patterns of Latin and English.
comments: Example: describing differences in expressions of indirect statements in Latin and English

A6F06082B6034EA99459584FD08A056E.description: Describe the influences of Roman history on today's world.
comments: Examples: television series Rome; the movies Gladiator, Cleopatra, and Troy; archeological discoveries

EFCA996CD45C4A778D7A6B2E9633F0CB.description: Describe Latin influences on other disciplines, including English and Romance languages, history, and philosophy.
comments: Examples: influence of Epicurean and Stoic philosophies on contemporary ideas and literature, current study of Julius Caesar's military tactics

709C280814E444FEB9523134B2358E1C.description: Locate historically important cities, countries, and geographical features of the ancient Mediterranean world.
comments: Examples: cities—Carthage, Troy, Alexandria, Athens, Delphi, Constantinople; countries—division of Gaul, Phoenicia, Magna Graecia, Crete, Sicily; geographical features—Rubicon, Po, Nile, Rhine, Alps, Pyrenees
Example: actions of Marius, Sulla, Cicero, and Cincinnatus
4AE655FB5D7F4B058DF2ED8E1EB4FFE1.description: Explain differences in the actions of legendary Roman heroes and those of historical Roman figures.

76F3240153274E77B77F0AB201049BBD.description: Explain the significance of people, events, and political terms in Roman history.
comments: Examples: people—early heroes, Sulla, Marius, Pompey, Caesar, Antony, Octavian, Constantine, Justinian; events—founding of Rome by Etruscans, plebeian struggle, Punic Wars, civil wars; political terms—monarchy, republic, laws, political parties, cursus honorum, First and Second Triumvirates

CA633134BF144DB2B64F59843B38A9D5.description: Recite passages in Latin using correct pronunciation and proper phrasing.
comments: Examples: United States Pledge of Allegiance in Latin, introduction to Caesar's De Bello Gallico

BFE1FAF52D6B4988AE51218FDE523528.description: Answer questions demonstrating comprehension and interpretation of Latin phrases and passages.

C1C9D0F9A89649A68870FC36BF4D2531.description: Use Level II Latin grammar and syntax to read and write Latin passages.
comments: Examples: fourth- and fifth-declension nouns and case usage, including genitive—partitive, description, object of certain adjectives and verbs, with causa or gratia to show purpose; dative—object of special verbs and compound verbs, purpose, reference, possession, dative of agent; accusative—place to which, subject of the indirect statement, with ad to show purpose; ablative—absolute, causal, object of deponent verbs, description, comparison, separation, respect, place from which, degree of difference; locative; indefinite and intensive pronouns; comparison of adjectives and adverbs; uses of quam with comparison of adjectives; irregular verbs, deponent verbs, participles, three tenses active and passive infinitives, four uses of infinitives, gerunds, gerundives, active and passive periphrastic, indirect statement; present and imperfect tenses of the subjunctive, volitive subjunctive, purpose, result subjunctive clauses; vocabulary learned in the dictionary format

9738D784051948A5B11A9397F435C7C5.description: List professional fields that employ Latin terminology.
comments: Examples: medical, legal, pharmacological, mathematical, scientific

F514BA3325F744A2B972280F7AD1D39D.description: Identify similarities of the culture of the United States to that of the Roman world, including architecture, daily life, and themes and heroes of classical mythology.

A5439ACB60BE405CB48E030E11AAB3AF.description: Recognize Latin derivatives, cognates, and language patterns, including mottoes, phrases, and abbreviations used in English.

9E5BD7D823384E1BA07E8B44164ACB1D.description: Identify evidence of contributions of Roman civilization and language to diverse cultures.
comments: Examples: Roman architectural sites in the Middle East, North Africa, and Europe; artistic interpretation of classical themes during the Renaissance

89F8E678DE294078B17F7EA40AB09592.description: Identify Latin influences on other disciplines.
comments: Examples: mathematics—Roman numerals, prefixes in metric system; science—terminology used in anatomy, names of planets used in astronomy

Examples: cities—Rome, Pompeii, Capua, Ostia, Brundisium; geographical features—Tiber, Arno, Po, Appian Way, Etruria, Britannia, Gallia, Germania, Graecia, Mare Nostrum, Aegean Sea, Adriatic Sea, Alps
E2AF5980C2FC44EB93388E4AADF00223.description: Locate historically important cities and major geographical features of Italy and western Europe.

264DF8EBFE13473A9BD7BBC8087C8134.description: Describe the most important Greco-Roman deities, including their characteristics, duties, and associated myths.
comments: Examples: Olympian gods, earth gods, mythical monsters, creation stories

DD438DCC1E174F14A64EB8532ACFA513.description: Describe elements of Roman daily life.
comments: Examples: calendar, religion, government, social organization, food, clothing, architecture, entertainment, recreation

BAD2369CDA6B4DBC9001B7A9D5ECAECE.description: Use correct pronunciation to read Latin sentences and phrases.

7BB4F280092B43C3A503BA783A170BCE.description: Respond orally to simple Latin sentences and phrases.

5BFB5AAF04734D5EAB22E16AE63EB367.description: Use Level I Latin grammar and syntax to read and write Latin.
comments: Examples: first-, second-, and third-declension nouns; six cases and their uses, including nominative—subject and predicate nominative; genitive—possession; dative—indirect object, with special adjectives; accusative—direct object, object of prepositions, duration of time, extent of space; ablative—manner, means, agent, accompaniment, place where, object of preposition, time when, within which; vocative—noun of direct address; first-, second-, and third-declension adjectives; personal, reflexive, relative, demonstrative, and interrogative pronouns; six tenses of verbs, four conjugations, active and passive voice, sum, possum; imperatives; present and perfect tense infinitives; vocabulary learned in the dictionary format

C53374424E2C450DA833B5E9C760FC10.description: Utilize language skills and cultural knowledge to demonstrate practical life applications.
comments: Examples: communicating with a pen pal, writing college admission essays, completing job applications

0C4666C782994CC39F120DF8CD7DA609.description: Create authentic cultural activities for a target culture event.
comments: Examples: dance performances, fairs, virtual tours
